Map of cumulative COVID-19 death rates by US state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-USmap-1)

The [CDC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention") publishes official numbers of COVID-19 cases in the United States. The CDC estimates that, between February 2020 and September 2021, only 1 in 1.3 COVID-19 deaths were attributed to COVID-19.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-2) The true COVID-19 death toll in the United States would therefore be higher than official reports, as modeled by a paper published in _The Lancet Regional Health - Americas_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-3) One way to estimate COVID-19 deaths that includes unconfirmed cases is to use the [excess mortality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excess_mortality "Excess mortality"), which is the overall number of deaths that exceed what would normally be expected.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-4) From March 1, 2020, through the end of 2020, there were 522,368 excess deaths in the United States, or 22.9% more deaths than would have been expected in that time period.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-5)

In February 2020, at the beginning of the pandemic, a shortage of tests made it impossible to confirm all possible COVID-19 cases[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-6) and resulting deaths, so the early numbers were likely undercounts.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Kliff+Bosman-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-10)

The following numbers are based on CDC data, which is incomplete.

## Measuring case and mortality rates

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/COVID19_deceased_in_Hackensack_NJ_April_27.jpg/250px-COVID19_deceased_in_Hackensack_NJ_April_27.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:COVID19_deceased_in_Hackensack_NJ_April_27.jpg)

Deceased persons in a 53-foot "mobile morgue" outside a hospital in [Hackensack, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hackensack,_New_Jersey "Hackensack, New Jersey") on April 27, 2020

In early 2020, deaths from all causes exceeded the seasonal average,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-:0nytimes-11) and data from early 2020 suggest additional deaths that were not counted in official reported coronavirus mortality statistics.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-12) Until February 28, 2020, CDC testing protocols allowed tests only for people who had traveled to China.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-13) In most U.S. locations, testing for some time was performed only on symptomatic people with a history of travel to Wuhan or with close contact to such people.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Madrigal-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-McFall_testing-16) The numbers were reported every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday and were split into categories: individual travelers, people who contracted the disease from other people within the U.S., and repatriated citizens who returned to the U.S. from crisis locations, such as Wuhan, where the disease originated, and the cruise ship _Diamond Princess_.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-17)

By March 26, 2020, the United States, with the world's third-largest population, surpassed China and Italy as the country with the world's highest number of confirmed cases.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-18) By April 25, the U.S. had more than 905,000 confirmed coronavirus cases and nearly 52,000 deaths, giving it a mortality rate around 5.7 percent. (In comparison, Spain's mortality rate was 10.2 percent and Italy's was 13.5 percent.)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-statista-20)

In April 2020, more than 10,000 American deaths had occurred in nursing homes. Most nursing homes did not have easy access to testing, making the actual number unknown.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-21) President Trump established a Coronavirus Commission for Safety and Quality in Nursing Homes.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-seniors-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-seniors-2-23) Subsequently, a number of states including Maryland[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-24) and New Jersey[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-25) reported their own estimates of deaths at nursing homes, ranging from twenty to fifty percent of the states' total deaths. A _[PNAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PNAS "PNAS")_ report in September 2020 confirmed that the virus is much more dangerous for the elderly than the young, noting that about 70% of all U.S. COVID-19 deaths had occurred to those over the age of 70.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-26)

As of early August 2020, among the 45 countries that had over 50,000 cases, the U.S. had the eighth highest number of deaths per-capita. Its [case fatality ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Case_fatality_rate "Case fatality rate"), however, was significantly better where it ranked 24th in the world, with 3.3% of its cases resulting in death.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-fatality-ratio-27) Several studies suggested that the number of infections was far higher than officially reported, and thus that the [infection fatality rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Case_fatality_rate#Infection_fatality_rate "Case fatality rate") was far lower than the [case fatality rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Case_fatality_rate "Case fatality rate").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-29)

The CDC estimates that 40% of people infected never show symptoms (i.e. are asymptomatic),[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-asymptomaticPct-30) although there is a 75% chance they can still spread the disease. And while children have a lower risk of becoming ill or dying, the CDC warns that they can still function as asymptomatic carriers and transmit the virus to adults.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-asymptomaticPct-30) The [American Academy of Pediatrics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Academy_of_Pediatrics "American Academy of Pediatrics")'s weekly report[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-AAP.org-weekly-31) from when states started reporting to September 17, 2020, tracked 587,948 child COVID-19 cases, 5,016 child hospitalizations, and 109 child deaths.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-AAP.org-Sept19-2020-32)

Epidemiologists depend on accurate reporting of cases and deaths to advise government response,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-33) and some have questioned the reliability of the numbers of confirmed cases.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-34) Rates differ among U.S. states, and there are also racial and economic disparities.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-U.S._News_and_World_Report-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-The_Print-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-University_of_Minnesota-37) After a group of epidemiologists requested revisions in how the CDC counts cases and deaths, the CDC in mid-April 2020 updated its guidance for counting COVID-19 cases and deaths to recommend that U.S. states report both confirmed and probable ones, though the decision is left to each state.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-38)

On September 25, 2020, _The Lancet_ published the largest study at the time to measure COVID-19 antibody levels in the US population, finding that less than ten percent of the U.S. population had been exposed.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Weintraub_2020-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-41) The study was published at a time when, according to _Newsweek_, "some U.S. officials have floated the concept of herd immunity as a possible strategy to manage the national outbreak,"[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Czachor_2020-42) and according to the lead author of the study, Stanford Center for Tubulointerstitial Kidney Disease director Shuchi Anand, "this study does not support that there is herd immunity."[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Feuer_2020-43) The research also uncovered racial and economic disparities in populations with COVID-19 antibodies[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Cortez_Sept_28_2020-44)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-U.S._News_and_World_Report-35) and highlighted the need for public health intervention to address the disparities.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-The_Print-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-University_of_Minnesota-37) At the time of the publication of the study, Anand announced that researchers would monitor the study participants for months to help determine the effectiveness of COVID-19 mitigation tactics.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Czachor_2020-42)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Cortez_Sept_28_2020-44)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Weintraub_2020-40)

As of May 2021[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States&action=edit), the [Centers for Disease Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control "Centers for Disease Control") estimated that there had been approximately 120 million infections in the United States.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-45)

According to the Center for Systems Science and Engineering (CSSE) at Johns Hopkins University as of 19:21 Eastern Standard Time (EST) on August 7, 2021, the total COVID-19 cases in the US had crossed the 35.73 million mark, with the death toll reaching 616,712.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-46)

## Death projections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Death projections")]

On March 31, 2020, the CDC projected that eventually 100,000–240,000 Americans would die of coronavirus.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-54) The lower end of the estimate was reached within two months after the CDC made its projection,[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-55) and the upper end was surpassed in November 2020.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-56) It is hard to say if the projections were accurate as some of the time they were, while others were very much off, however it was hard to predict the amount of deaths when new variants like the [Omicron variant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SARS-CoV-2_Omicron_variant "SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant") and the [Delta variant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SARS-CoV-2_Delta_variant "SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant") were rising.

The CDC uses an [ensemble forecast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ensemble_forecasting "Ensemble forecasting"), meaning it receives predictions from multiple sources and aggregates them to make its own forecast. As of December 2020, the CDC included 37 modeling groups in its ensemble forecast and was predicting the death toll 4 weeks in advance.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-57)

Examples:

*   At the end of May 2020, the CDC correctly projected the death toll would surpass 115,000 by June 20.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-59)
*   At the end of July 2020, the CDC correctly projected the death toll would surpass 168,000 by August 22.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-CDCforecasts-60)
*   In mid-October 2020, the CDC correctly projected the death toll would reach 230,000–250,000 by mid-November.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-CDCforecasts-60)

In mid-February 2021, when the death toll had already reached 470,000,[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-61) the [IHME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_for_Health_Metrics_and_Evaluation "Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation") projected that the death toll would reach 600,000 by June 1.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-62) However, the death rate dropped during this time period and the total death toll on June 1 was not as high as expected, having reached only about 592,000.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-63) The total of 600,000 was reached two weeks later.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-64)

In mid-September 2021, when the death toll had already reached 670,000, the IHME projected that the death toll would reach 775,000 by the end of the year.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-65) That number was reached by the end of November 2021.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-66)

On January 12, 2022, when the death toll had already reached 842,000, a CDC ensemble forecast predicted that 62,000 people would die over the next four weeks.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-67)

At the start of January 2023, when the US death toll had accumulated to over 1,120,000, the IHME projected that the death toll would reach 1,130,000 by April 1.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-68)

## Comparisons

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Comparisons")]

Epidemics of similar size (the number is the U.S. death toll):

*   [HIV/AIDS in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS_in_the_United_States "HIV/AIDS in the United States"): 700,000 as of 2018[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States&action=edit)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-69)
*   [1918 Spanish Flu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_flu "Spanish flu"): 675,000[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-CDC_past-70)

Other large epidemics:

*   [1957–1958 influenza pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1957%E2%80%931958_influenza_pandemic "1957–1958 influenza pandemic"): 116,000[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-CDC_past-70)
*   [1968 Hong Kong flu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_flu "Hong Kong flu"): 100,000[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-CDC_past-70)

Main article: COVID-19 pandemic in the United States

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Timeline_of_weekly_confirmed_COVID-19_deaths_in_the_United_States.svg/500px-Timeline_of_weekly_confirmed_COVID-19_deaths_in_the_United_States.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Timeline_of_weekly_confirmed_COVID-19_deaths_in_the_United_States.svg)

Weekly confirmed COVID-19 deaths

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/39/Map_of_cumulative_COVID-19_death_rates_by_US_state.png/500px-Map_of_cumulative_COVID-19_death_rates_by_US_state.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Map_of_cumulative_COVID-19_death_rates_by_US_state.png)

Map of cumulative COVID-19 death rates by US state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-USmap-1)

The [CDC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention") publishes official numbers of COVID-19 cases in the United States. The CDC estimates that, between February 2020 and September 2021, only 1 in 1.3 COVID-19 deaths were attributed to COVID-19.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-2) The true COVID-19 death toll in the United States would therefore be higher than official reports, as modeled by a paper published in _The Lancet Regional Health - Americas_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-3) One way to estimate COVID-19 deaths that includes unconfirmed cases is to use the [excess mortality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excess_mortality "Excess mortality"), which is the overall number of deaths that exceed what would normally be expected.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-4) From March 1, 2020, through the end of 2020, there were 522,368 excess deaths in the United States, or 22.9% more deaths than would have been expected in that time period.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-5)

In February 2020, at the beginning of the pandemic, a shortage of tests made it impossible to confirm all possible COVID-19 cases[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-6) and resulting deaths, so the early numbers were likely undercounts.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Kliff+Bosman-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-10)

The following numbers are based on CDC data, which is incomplete.

## Measuring case and mortality rates

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Measuring case and mortality rates")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/COVID19_deceased_in_Hackensack_NJ_April_27.jpg/250px-COVID19_deceased_in_Hackensack_NJ_April_27.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:COVID19_deceased_in_Hackensack_NJ_April_27.jpg)

Deceased persons in a 53-foot "mobile morgue" outside a hospital in [Hackensack, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hackensack,_New_Jersey "Hackensack, New Jersey") on April 27, 2020

In early 2020, deaths from all causes exceeded the seasonal average,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-:0nytimes-11) and data from early 2020 suggest additional deaths that were not counted in official reported coronavirus mortality statistics.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-12) Until February 28, 2020, CDC testing protocols allowed tests only for people who had traveled to China.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-13) In most U.S. locations, testing for some time was performed only on symptomatic people with a history of travel to Wuhan or with close contact to such people.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Madrigal-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-McFall_testing-16) The numbers were reported every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday and were split into categories: individual travelers, people who contracted the disease from other people within the U.S., and repatriated citizens who returned to the U.S. from crisis locations, such as Wuhan, where the disease originated, and the cruise ship _Diamond Princess_.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-17)

By March 26, 2020, the United States, with the world's third-largest population, surpassed China and Italy as the country with the world's highest number of confirmed cases.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-18) By April 25, the U.S. had more than 905,000 confirmed coronavirus cases and nearly 52,000 deaths, giving it a mortality rate around 5.7 percent. (In comparison, Spain's mortality rate was 10.2 percent and Italy's was 13.5 percent.)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-statista-20)

In April 2020, more than 10,000 American deaths had occurred in nursing homes. Most nursing homes did not have easy access to testing, making the actual number unknown.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-21) President Trump established a Coronavirus Commission for Safety and Quality in Nursing Homes.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-seniors-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-seniors-2-23) Subsequently, a number of states including Maryland[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-24) and New Jersey[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-25) reported their own estimates of deaths at nursing homes, ranging from twenty to fifty percent of the states' total deaths. A _[PNAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PNAS "PNAS")_ report in September 2020 confirmed that the virus is much more dangerous for the elderly than the young, noting that about 70% of all U.S. COVID-19 deaths had occurred to those over the age of 70.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-26)

As of early August 2020, among the 45 countries that had over 50,000 cases, the U.S. had the eighth highest number of deaths per-capita. Its [case fatality ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Case_fatality_rate "Case fatality rate"), however, was significantly better where it ranked 24th in the world, with 3.3% of its cases resulting in death.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-fatality-ratio-27) Several studies suggested that the number of infections was far higher than officially reported, and thus that the [infection fatality rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Case_fatality_rate#Infection_fatality_rate "Case fatality rate") was far lower than the [case fatality rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Case_fatality_rate "Case fatality rate").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-29)

The CDC estimates that 40% of people infected never show symptoms (i.e. are asymptomatic),[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-asymptomaticPct-30) although there is a 75% chance they can still spread the disease. And while children have a lower risk of becoming ill or dying, the CDC warns that they can still function as asymptomatic carriers and transmit the virus to adults.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-asymptomaticPct-30) The [American Academy of Pediatrics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Academy_of_Pediatrics "American Academy of Pediatrics")'s weekly report[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-AAP.org-weekly-31) from when states started reporting to September 17, 2020, tracked 587,948 child COVID-19 cases, 5,016 child hospitalizations, and 109 child deaths.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-AAP.org-Sept19-2020-32)

Epidemiologists depend on accurate reporting of cases and deaths to advise government response,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-33) and some have questioned the reliability of the numbers of confirmed cases.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-34) Rates differ among U.S. states, and there are also racial and economic disparities.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-U.S._News_and_World_Report-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-The_Print-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-University_of_Minnesota-37) After a group of epidemiologists requested revisions in how the CDC counts cases and deaths, the CDC in mid-April 2020 updated its guidance for counting COVID-19 cases and deaths to recommend that U.S. states report both confirmed and probable ones, though the decision is left to each state.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-38)

On September 25, 2020, _The Lancet_ published the largest study at the time to measure COVID-19 antibody levels in the US population, finding that less than ten percent of the U.S. population had been exposed.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Weintraub_2020-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-41) The study was published at a time when, according to _Newsweek_, "some U.S. officials have floated the concept of herd immunity as a possible strategy to manage the national outbreak,"[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Czachor_2020-42) and according to the lead author of the study, Stanford Center for Tubulointerstitial Kidney Disease director Shuchi Anand, "this study does not support that there is herd immunity."[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Feuer_2020-43) The research also uncovered racial and economic disparities in populations with COVID-19 antibodies[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Cortez_Sept_28_2020-44)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-U.S._News_and_World_Report-35) and highlighted the need for public health intervention to address the disparities.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-The_Print-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-University_of_Minnesota-37) At the time of the publication of the study, Anand announced that researchers would monitor the study participants for months to help determine the effectiveness of COVID-19 mitigation tactics.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Czachor_2020-42)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Cortez_Sept_28_2020-44)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-Weintraub_2020-40)

As of May 2021[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States&action=edit), the [Centers for Disease Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control "Centers for Disease Control") estimated that there had been approximately 120 million infections in the United States.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-45)

According to the Center for Systems Science and Engineering (CSSE) at Johns Hopkins University as of 19:21 Eastern Standard Time (EST) on August 7, 2021, the total COVID-19 cases in the US had crossed the 35.73 million mark, with the death toll reaching 616,712.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-46)

## Death projections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Death projections")]

On March 31, 2020, the CDC projected that eventually 100,000–240,000 Americans would die of coronavirus.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-54) The lower end of the estimate was reached within two months after the CDC made its projection,[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-55) and the upper end was surpassed in November 2020.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-56) It is hard to say if the projections were accurate as some of the time they were, while others were very much off, however it was hard to predict the amount of deaths when new variants like the [Omicron variant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SARS-CoV-2_Omicron_variant "SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant") and the [Delta variant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SARS-CoV-2_Delta_variant "SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant") were rising.

The CDC uses an [ensemble forecast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ensemble_forecasting "Ensemble forecasting"), meaning it receives predictions from multiple sources and aggregates them to make its own forecast. As of December 2020, the CDC included 37 modeling groups in its ensemble forecast and was predicting the death toll 4 weeks in advance.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-57)

Examples:

*   At the end of May 2020, the CDC correctly projected the death toll would surpass 115,000 by June 20.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-59)
*   At the end of July 2020, the CDC correctly projected the death toll would surpass 168,000 by August 22.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-CDCforecasts-60)
*   In mid-October 2020, the CDC correctly projected the death toll would reach 230,000–250,000 by mid-November.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-CDCforecasts-60)

In mid-February 2021, when the death toll had already reached 470,000,[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-61) the [IHME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_for_Health_Metrics_and_Evaluation "Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation") projected that the death toll would reach 600,000 by June 1.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-62) However, the death rate dropped during this time period and the total death toll on June 1 was not as high as expected, having reached only about 592,000.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-63) The total of 600,000 was reached two weeks later.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-64)

In mid-September 2021, when the death toll had already reached 670,000, the IHME projected that the death toll would reach 775,000 by the end of the year.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-65) That number was reached by the end of November 2021.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-66)

On January 12, 2022, when the death toll had already reached 842,000, a CDC ensemble forecast predicted that 62,000 people would die over the next four weeks.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-67)

At the start of January 2023, when the US death toll had accumulated to over 1,120,000, the IHME projected that the death toll would reach 1,130,000 by April 1.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_of_the_COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States#cite_note-68)

*   Mortality rates are age-adjusted to account for differences in age distribution and population size between different populations.

## Sources

The [CDC WONDER](https://wonder.cdc.gov/) Online Database is the source of the 2024 [National Vital Statistics System](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/index.htm) death data featured in Stats of the States.

Where states are ranked, states are categorized from highest rate to lowest rate. Mortality rankings and rates are based on 2024 age-adjusted death rates.

**Keep Reading**[Age Standardization of Death Rates: Implementation of the Year 2000 Standard](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr47/nvs47_03.pdf)

Although adjusted for variations in age distribution and population size, differences by state do not account for other state-specific population characteristics that may affect death rates.

When the number of deaths is small, differences between states and rankings by state may be unreliable due to instability in rates.

## Key points

*   Find death (mortality) rates from COVID-19 for each state in map and table formats.
*   The mortality rate is the number of deaths per 100,000 total population.
*   Mortality rates are age-adjusted to account for differences in age distribution and population size between different populations.

## Sources

The [CDC WONDER](https://wonder.cdc.gov/) Online Database is the source of the 2024 [National Vital Statistics System](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/index.htm) death data featured in Stats of the States.

Where states are ranked, states are categorized from highest rate to lowest rate. Mortality rankings and rates are based on 2024 age-adjusted death rates.

**Keep Reading**[Age Standardization of Death Rates: Implementation of the Year 2000 Standard](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr47/nvs47_03.pdf)

Although adjusted for variations in age distribution and population size, differences by state do not account for other state-specific population characteristics that may affect death rates.

When the number of deaths is small, differences between states and rankings by state may be unreliable due to instability in rates.

# The color of coronavirus:  
COVID-19 deaths by race and ethnicity in the U.S.

![Image 3](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5c9542c8840b163998cf4804/1586384056475-MG2T5LC327PG90YP5A7I/corona-mask-mashup.PNG)

### **by**[ELISABETH GAWTHROP](https://www.apmresearchlab.org/authors#elisabeth)**| October 19, 2023**

* * *

### You value and rely on the work of the APM Research Lab. And we rely on you, especially   
during this difficult time. If you can, please support our work with a donation today.

[DONATE](https://support.americanpublicmedia.org/APMRL_web)

* * *

## RELATED CONTENT:

### ARCHIVE: [Past Color of Coronavirus updates](https://www.apmresearchlab.org/covid/deaths-by-race-archive)

### VACCINES: [How are states doing on COVID-19 vaccination efforts?](https://www.apmresearchlab.org/covid/vaccine-progress)

### COVID-19 in Minnesota: [Key data](https://www.apmresearchlab.org/covid/mn-key-data)

### **COVID-19 ALONG THE NATION’S SOUTHERN CORRIDOR:**[**What we’ve learned two+ years into the pandemic**](https://www.apmresearchlab.org/10x-covid-deaths-vax)

### LAB NOTE: [While still lower than most groups, COVID-19 deaths among white Americans have increased faster over the past three years](https://www.apmresearchlab.org/blog/while-still-lower-than-most-groups-white-covid-19-death-rates-have-increased-faster-than-other-groups)

The United States’ official [COVID-19 death toll is more than 1,147,000](https://covid.cdc.gov/covid-data-tracker/#trends_totaldeaths), with [estimates](https://www.bu.edu/articles/2022/covid-death-toll-higher-than-official-tally/)[suggesting](https://www.economist.com/graphic-detail/coronavirus-excess-deaths-estimates) that the true toll could be 20% higher. Our ongoing Color of Coronavirus project monitors how and where COVID-19 mortality is inequitably impacting certain communities, with an aim to help guide policy and community responses. Relying on data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, we have documented the race and ethnicity for 99% of these cumulative deaths in the United States.

The CDC has recently stopped updating the datasets used in this report, so it is unknown at this time if and when we will provide another update. Today’s update includes data through August, the last month for which there is a full month of data available.

We highlight national trends in this report, but state-level data is also available in the interactive graphics below and through our [GitHub](https://github.com/APM-Research-Lab/color-of-coronavirus). We’ve also created [an archive page](https://www.apmresearchlab.org/covid/deaths-by-race-archive) for past updates.

### Jump to: Recent Trends | Key Findings | Examine the Data

* * *

## RECENT TRENDS: Mortality rates dropped over summer for all racial and ethnic groups; white Americans have highest rates in most months of 2023

Our last update in June included data through April, which we reported as the month with the fewest deaths since the beginning of the pandemic. Mortality rates dropped further in the ensuing months across all race and ethnicity groups, until August, when deaths increased somewhat for all groups. The below graph shows monthly mortality rates by group since the beginning of 2023.

Made with Flourish•[Create a chart](https://flourish.studio/visualisations/line-bar-pie-charts/?utm_source=showcase&utm_campaign=visualisation/15421405)

July now ranks as the month with the fewest COVID-related deaths since the start of the pandemic, with 2,295 deaths associated with COVID-19. Deaths in August increased by 67% to 3,837. While comprehensive data for the full month of September is not available, [CDC trackers](https://covid.cdc.gov/covid-data-tracker/#trends_totaldeaths_select_00) indicate that deaths are now on the decline again.

Made with Flourish•[Create a chart](https://flourish.studio/visualisations/line-bar-pie-charts/?utm_source=showcase&utm_campaign=visualisation/15409596)

When considering the COVID death _rate_ in each racial and ethnic group, white Americans had the highest monthly crude mortality rate in August at 1.52 per 100,000. (The crude mortality rate is defined as the number of people with a certain racial or ethnic identity divided by the total population of people with that same racial or ethnic identity, usually reported per 100,00 people).

Pacific Islander Americans had the second-highest mortality rate at 1.14 per 100,000. Americans of more than one race had the lowest monthly crude mortality rate, with 0.24 per 100,000, and Latino Americans the second-lowest rate at 0.52 per 100,000.

Even with nearly 4,000 deaths in August, the drop in mortality rates compared to earlier in the pandemic is striking. For Black, Indigenous and Pacific Islander Americans, average monthly crude mortality rates since the beginning of 2023 have been about 10% of what they averaged for 2020, 2021 and 2022 combined, and for Latino Americans it is a bit lower at 8%. For Americans of more than one race and Asian Americans, the 2023 monthly mortality rate has been about 16% compared to the earlier years, which is close to the average for all Americans. And for white Americans, the monthly mortality rate in 2023 has been 19% of the previous years’ monthly rates.

Made with Flourish•[Create a chart](https://flourish.studio/visualisations/line-bar-pie-charts/?utm_source=showcase&utm_campaign=visualisation/15411720)

This year, the _cumulative_ white crude mortality rate became higher than all racial and ethnic groups except for Indigenous Americans (although it’s still just barely above Black and Pacific Islander Americans). An important caveat, however, is that the crude mortality rate numbers are not age-adjusted. After adjusting for age, white Americans have the second-_lowest_ mortality rate (see more below).

Made with Flourish•[Create a chart](https://flourish.studio/visualisations/line-bar-pie-charts/?utm_source=showcase&utm_campaign=visualisation/15409598)

Now, let’s turn to additional insights the latest data tells us about national mortality trends throughout the pandemic.

* * *

### See our work cited in [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2021/feb/04/native-americans-coronavirus-covid-death-rate), [The Atlantic](https://www.theatlantic.com/family/archive/2021/01/us-covid-19-death-toll/617544/), [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/brucejapsen/2020/06/12/obamacare-insurer-centene-boosts-pandemic-outlook-and-focus-on-health-disparities/#1531e48b3e24), [CNN](https://edition.cnn.com/2020/06/18/politics/anthony-brown-bill-racial-disparities-covid/index.html), [NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/science/science-news/cancer-alley-renewed-focus-systemic-racism-too-late-n1231602), [Vox](https://www.vox.com/2020/6/17/21284527/systemic-racism-black-americans-9-charts-explained), [JAMA](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2767029), [Politico](https://www.politico.com/news/2020/06/11/native-american-coronavirus-data-314527), [Newsweek](https://www.newsweek.com/ayanna-pressley-says-black-people-are-managing-pandemic-within-pandemic-when-it-comes-police-1508467), [Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/ajimpact/black-lives-matter-protests-spotlight-environmental-racism-200618200615984.html), the [Washington Post](https://www.washingtonpost.com/national/on-the-way-to-the-store-a-mask-giveaway-to-protect-african-americans-from-coronavirus/2020/05/15/dce4fc8a-970b-11ea-82b4-c8db161ff6e5_story.html), [The Hill](https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/499251-covid-19-makes-trumps-work-with-black-americans-that-much-harder), the [New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2020/06/07/us/politics/blacks-coronavirus-police-brutality.html) and [numerous other outlets](https://www.apmresearchlab.org/covid/media-mentions).

* * *

### Jump to: Recent Trends | Key Findings | Examine the Data

* * *

## KEY FINDINGS (from data updated September 27, 2023):

_Note: these numbers are sourced from this_[_CDC dataset_](https://data.cdc.gov/NCHS/Distribution-of-COVID-19-Deaths-and-Populations-by/jwta-jxbg)_, the total count of which sometimes differs slightly from the total count reported on the_[_CDC’s primary mortality landing page_](https://covid.cdc.gov/covid-data-tracker/#datatracker-home)_. Also, time series data used in this report’s figures lags behind these cumulative numbers due to incompleteness of recent data._

*   Of the approximately 1,147,000 cumulative official COVID-19 deaths in the U.S., these are the numbers of lives lost by group:**Asian (35,967), Black (157,169), Indigenous (12,122), Latino (172,235), Pacific Islander (2,323) and white Americans (759,258). Additionally, (7,613) deaths are recorded as “other race”.**

*   These are the documented, nationwide (U.S. states + D.C.) crude mortality rates (not age-adjusted) from COVID-19 data for all racial and ethnic groups since the start of the pandemic.

    *   **1 in 201 Indigenous Americans have died** (or 498 deaths per 100,000)

    *   **1 in 259 white Americans have died** (or 386 deaths per 100,000)

    *   **1 in 264 Black Americans have died** (or 379 deaths per 100,000)

    *   **1 in 264 Pacific Islander Americans have died** (or 379 deaths per 100,000)

    *   **1 in 356 Latino Americans have died** (or 281 deaths per 100,000)

    *   **1 in 538 Asian Americans have died**(or 186 deaths per 100,000)

*   **Indigenous Americans have the highest crude COVID-19 mortality rate nationwide**— about 2.7 times as high as the rate for Asian Americans, who have the lowest crude rate. And, the CDC notes that Indigenous American deaths are often undercounted, with the [latest research](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr70/NVSR70-12.pdf) suggesting the true mortality rate for this group could be around 34% higher than official reports.

*   Because the risk of COVID-19 mortality increases with age, it is important to consider the varying age distributions of America's racial and ethnic groups. A higher share of white Americans are in the older age brackets than any other group. And even within the same race groups, the age distribution varies by location—with retirement destination states such as Florida having a much higher share of older adults within their white population, for example. **Indigenous, Latino, Pacific Islander and Black Americans all have significantly higher COVID-19 mortality rates than either white or Asian Americans once the data are adjusted to account for age distribution differences among racial and ethnic groups**.Nationally, every group except for white Americans has a higher mortality rate after accounting for age, and**Latino Americans see the greatest increase in mortality when converting crude rates to age-adjusted rates.**

## **_What about the difference between deaths directly and indirectly caused by COVID-19?_**

**_To cut through the complications around definitions of a “COVID-19 death”, we compiled_**[**_excess mortality from the last six years, by state_**](https://www.apmresearchlab.org/covid/excess-mortality-by-state-graphics)**_. Although it doesn’t specifically include race and ethnicity, it affirms the time-related patterns we’ve seen in the analyses for this update. At one extreme, for example, New York sees its worst wave in the spring of 2020, while at the other, Vermont’s excess mortality is consistently highest in 2022._**

Age adjusting is a common and important tool that health researchers use when diseases carry varying levels of risk depending on age. Age adjusting allows for a more apples-to-apples comparison among racial and ethnic groups because, in the case of COVID-19, risks are higher for older populations, and racial and ethnic groups in the U.S. have differing proportions of older populations relative to the rest of their populations. As [noted by the CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/covid-data/investigations-discovery/hospitalization-death-by-race-ethnicity.html), “adjusting by age is important because risk of infection, hospitalization, and death is different by age, and age distribution differs by racial and ethnic group. If the effect of age is not accounted for, racial and ethnic disparities can be underestimated or overestimated.”

We’ve included some key assumptions and caveats, as well as an explanation of age adjusting, at the bottom of the page and we’ve made our full code and methods available on our [GitHub repository](https://github.com/APM-Research-Lab/color-of-coronavirus).

##### NOTES

###### **Racial and Ethnic Groups**  
Our labels of each racial or ethnic group correspond as follows: *   Latino — Hispanic or Latino ethnicity of any race
*   Pacific Islander — Non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander
*   Indigenous — Non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native
*   White — Non-Hispanic white
*   Black — Non-Hispanic Black or African American 
*   Asian — Non-Hispanic Asian 
*   More than one race — Non-Hispanic more than one race

###### As noted above, Indigenous American deaths [are known](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr70/NVSR70-12.pdf) to be underreported by 34%. [According to the CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/vsrr/covid19/tech_notes.htm), deaths are also known to be underreported for non-Hispanic API (3%) and for Hispanic decedents (3%).

###### Some CDC datasets include a "more than one race" racial category and some include an "other" category. We have included the data that indicates more than one race when available, for which there is also an overall population figure available as a denominator when calculating rates. No such denominator is available for calculating rates for the "other" category. The deaths listed in the "other" category constitute less than 1% of total reported deaths.

###### **Age-Adjusted Rates**  
 While there are many features of the novel coronavirus that are still unclear, this we know with certainty: The risk of dying from COVID-19 rises sharply with advanced age. [According to the CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/covid-data/investigations-discovery/hospitalization-death-by-age.html), people 65-74 years old have 65 times the risk of dying from COVID-19 compared to people aged 18-29. That risk increases to 140 times higher for people in the 75-84 age bracket, and 340 times for people age 85 or older.   
  
 Due to this steep age gradient to COVID-19 mortality, it is important to consider the varying age distributions of America's racial and ethnic groups. A higher share of white Americans are in the older age brackets than any other group. And even within the same race groups, the age distribution varies by location—with retirement destination states such as Florida having a much higher share of older adults within their white population, for example.   
  
 To remove the role of these age differences from COVID-19 mortality rates, we have also produced age-adjusted rates. There are two main categories of methods used to produce age-adjusted rates: direct and indirect standardization. The direct method uses the age distribution of COVID-19 deaths within a racial or ethnic group, while the indirect method takes the total number of COVID-19 deaths within a racial ethnic group and applies mortality rates by age group from the national level (all races) to the age distribution of that racial or ethnic group.   
  
 We have used the direct method where possible, but the direct method requires knowing the numbers of deaths for each age grouping for each race and, when calculating at the state level, for each state. For states with smaller populations, there are instances where not all of the age groupings reach the threshold of at least 10 to be released by CDC. For these suppressed groups/places, we have used the indirect method to calculate an age-adjusted rate.   
  
 To evaluate the accuracy of the indirectly age-adjusted rates, we compared direct and indirect rates where possible. Most indirect rates were within 5% of the direct rates. Some were up to 10% different and two were approaching 15% different. The higher errors tended to be for groups/places with lower numbers of COVID-19 deaths. For this reason, we chose to not calculate indirect rates for groups/places with fewer than 200 COVID-19 deaths. The indirect rates tended to be higher than the direct rates, but not universally.   
  
 All of these numbers are available for download on our [GitHub](https://github.com/APM-Research-Lab), including an indication of whether the age-adjustment for a particular group/place has been directly or indirectly calculated.   
  
 What do the results of these calculations mean? The age-adjusted rates indicate that many younger Americans who are Black, Latino, Indigenous or Pacific Islanders are dying of COVID-19—driving their mortality rates far above that of white and Asian Americans. Despite their relative youthfulness (a protective factor against COVID), their death rates are elevated.   
  
 It is important to note that, while age-adjusted mortality rates help us remove the influence of age differences in racial groups to examine disparities in outcomes, they are not the actual mortality rates experienced by these groups.

The United States’ official [COVID-19 death toll is more than 1,147,000](https://covid.cdc.gov/covid-data-tracker/#trends_totaldeaths), with [estimates](https://www.bu.edu/articles/2022/covid-death-toll-higher-than-official-tally/)[suggesting](https://www.economist.com/graphic-detail/coronavirus-excess-deaths-estimates) that the true toll could be 20% higher. Our ongoing Color of Coronavirus project monitors how and where COVID-19 mortality is inequitably impacting certain communities, with an aim to help guide policy and community responses. Relying on data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, we have documented the race and ethnicity for 99% of these cumulative deaths in the United States.

The CDC has recently stopped updating the datasets used in this report, so it is unknown at this time if and when we will provide another update. Today’s update includes data through August, the last month for which there is a full month of data available.

We highlight national trends in this report, but state-level data is also available in the interactive graphics below and through our [GitHub](https://github.com/APM-Research-Lab/color-of-coronavirus). We’ve also created [an archive page](https://www.apmresearchlab.org/covid/deaths-by-race-archive) for past updates.

## RECENT TRENDS: Mortality rates dropped over summer for all racial and ethnic groups; white Americans have highest rates in most months of 2023

Our last update in June included data through April, which we reported as the month with the fewest deaths since the beginning of the pandemic. Mortality rates dropped further in the ensuing months across all race and ethnicity groups, until August, when deaths increased somewhat for all groups. The below graph shows monthly mortality rates by group since the beginning of 2023.

Made with Flourish•[Create a chart](https://flourish.studio/visualisations/line-bar-pie-charts/?utm_source=showcase&utm_campaign=visualisation/15421405)

July now ranks as the month with the fewest COVID-related deaths since the start of the pandemic, with 2,295 deaths associated with COVID-19. Deaths in August increased by 67% to 3,837. While comprehensive data for the full month of September is not available, [CDC trackers](https://covid.cdc.gov/covid-data-tracker/#trends_totaldeaths_select_00) indicate that deaths are now on the decline again.

Made with Flourish•[Create a chart](https://flourish.studio/visualisations/line-bar-pie-charts/?utm_source=showcase&utm_campaign=visualisation/15409596)

When considering the COVID death _rate_ in each racial and ethnic group, white Americans had the highest monthly crude mortality rate in August at 1.52 per 100,000. (The crude mortality rate is defined as the number of people with a certain racial or ethnic identity divided by the total population of people with that same racial or ethnic identity, usually reported per 100,00 people).

Pacific Islander Americans had the second-highest mortality rate at 1.14 per 100,000. Americans of more than one race had the lowest monthly crude mortality rate, with 0.24 per 100,000, and Latino Americans the second-lowest rate at 0.52 per 100,000.

Even with nearly 4,000 deaths in August, the drop in mortality rates compared to earlier in the pandemic is striking. For Black, Indigenous and Pacific Islander Americans, average monthly crude mortality rates since the beginning of 2023 have been about 10% of what they averaged for 2020, 2021 and 2022 combined, and for Latino Americans it is a bit lower at 8%. For Americans of more than one race and Asian Americans, the 2023 monthly mortality rate has been about 16% compared to the earlier years, which is close to the average for all Americans. And for white Americans, the monthly mortality rate in 2023 has been 19% of the previous years’ monthly rates.

Made with Flourish•[Create a chart](https://flourish.studio/visualisations/line-bar-pie-charts/?utm_source=showcase&utm_campaign=visualisation/15411720)

This year, the _cumulative_ white crude mortality rate became higher than all racial and ethnic groups except for Indigenous Americans (although it’s still just barely above Black and Pacific Islander Americans). An important caveat, however, is that the crude mortality rate numbers are not age-adjusted. After adjusting for age, white Americans have the second-_lowest_ mortality rate (see more below).

Made with Flourish•[Create a chart](https://flourish.studio/visualisations/line-bar-pie-charts/?utm_source=showcase&utm_campaign=visualisation/15409598)

Now, let’s turn to additional insights the latest data tells us about national mortality trends throughout the pandemic.

## KEY FINDINGS (from data updated September 27, 2023):

_Note: these numbers are sourced from this_[_CDC dataset_](https://data.cdc.gov/NCHS/Distribution-of-COVID-19-Deaths-and-Populations-by/jwta-jxbg)_, the total count of which sometimes differs slightly from the total count reported on the_[_CDC’s primary mortality landing page_](https://covid.cdc.gov/covid-data-tracker/#datatracker-home)_. Also, time series data used in this report’s figures lags behind these cumulative numbers due to incompleteness of recent data._

*   Of the approximately 1,147,000 cumulative official COVID-19 deaths in the U.S., these are the numbers of lives lost by group:**Asian (35,967), Black (157,169), Indigenous (12,122), Latino (172,235), Pacific Islander (2,323) and white Americans (759,258). Additionally, (7,613) deaths are recorded as “other race”.**

*   These are the documented, nationwide (U.S. states + D.C.) crude mortality rates (not age-adjusted) from COVID-19 data for all racial and ethnic groups since the start of the pandemic.

    *   **1 in 201 Indigenous Americans have died** (or 498 deaths per 100,000)

    *   **1 in 259 white Americans have died** (or 386 deaths per 100,000)

    *   **1 in 264 Black Americans have died** (or 379 deaths per 100,000)

    *   **1 in 264 Pacific Islander Americans have died** (or 379 deaths per 100,000)

    *   **1 in 356 Latino Americans have died** (or 281 deaths per 100,000)

    *   **1 in 538 Asian Americans have died**(or 186 deaths per 100,000)

*   **Indigenous Americans have the highest crude COVID-19 mortality rate nationwide**— about 2.7 times as high as the rate for Asian Americans, who have the lowest crude rate. And, the CDC notes that Indigenous American deaths are often undercounted, with the [latest research](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr70/NVSR70-12.pdf) suggesting the true mortality rate for this group could be around 34% higher than official reports.

*   Because the risk of COVID-19 mortality increases with age, it is important to consider the varying age distributions of America's racial and ethnic groups. A higher share of white Americans are in the older age brackets than any other group. And even within the same race groups, the age distribution varies by location—with retirement destination states such as Florida having a much higher share of older adults within their white population, for example. **Indigenous, Latino, Pacific Islander and Black Americans all have significantly higher COVID-19 mortality rates than either white or Asian Americans once the data are adjusted to account for age distribution differences among racial and ethnic groups**.Nationally, every group except for white Americans has a higher mortality rate after accounting for age, and**Latino Americans see the greatest increase in mortality when converting crude rates to age-adjusted rates.**

## **_What about the difference between deaths directly and indirectly caused by COVID-19?_**

**_To cut through the complications around definitions of a “COVID-19 death”, we compiled_**[**_excess mortality from the last six years, by state_**](https://www.apmresearchlab.org/covid/excess-mortality-by-state-graphics)**_. Although it doesn’t specifically include race and ethnicity, it affirms the time-related patterns we’ve seen in the analyses for this update. At one extreme, for example, New York sees its worst wave in the spring of 2020, while at the other, Vermont’s excess mortality is consistently highest in 2022._**

Age adjusting is a common and important tool that health researchers use when diseases carry varying levels of risk depending on age. Age adjusting allows for a more apples-to-apples comparison among racial and ethnic groups because, in the case of COVID-19, risks are higher for older populations, and racial and ethnic groups in the U.S. have differing proportions of older populations relative to the rest of their populations. As [noted by the CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/covid-data/investigations-discovery/hospitalization-death-by-race-ethnicity.html), “adjusting by age is important because risk of infection, hospitalization, and death is different by age, and age distribution differs by racial and ethnic group. If the effect of age is not accounted for, racial and ethnic disparities can be underestimated or overestimated.”

We’ve included some key assumptions and caveats, as well as an explanation of age adjusting, at the bottom of the page and we’ve made our full code and methods available on our [GitHub repository](https://github.com/APM-Research-Lab/color-of-coronavirus).

## FOCUS ON ASIAN AMERICANS

### Lives lost to date

*   35,967 Asian Americans are known to have lost their lives to COVID-19 through September 27, 2023. There were 137 new deaths reported among Asian Americans for the last full month of data (August 2023), which is a 41% increase from the preceding month (97 deaths).

*   Nationwide, Asian Americans have experienced 3.1% of all deaths, while they represent 5.9% of the population.

### Crude mortality rate

*   For every 100,000 Asian Americans, about 186 have died from the coronavirus, a mortality rate lower than all other racial or ethnic groups.

*   In 11 states, more than 1 in 500 Asian American residents have died from COVID-19 (i.e., more than 200 per 100,000).

### Age-adjusted mortality rate

*   Nationwide, Asian Americans have the lowest age-adjusted mortality rate (228 per 100,000), followed by white Americans (315).

*   Once adjusted for age, the highest COVID-19 mortality rates for Asian Americans are in Minnesota (399), Nevada (394), New York (364), Wisconsin (358) and Arizona (282).

Note: Nationwide statistics are derived from CDC reporting at the national level and are not suppressed. State level statistics are suppressed by CDC when the number of deaths is between 1-9.

## FOCUS ON BLACK AMERICANS

### Lives lost to date

*   157,169 Black Americans are known to have lost their lives to COVID-19 through September 27, 2023. There were 337 new deaths reported among Black Americans for the last full month of data (August 2023), which is a 58% increase from deaths in the preceding month (213).

*   Nationwide, Black Americans have experienced 13.7% of all deaths, while they represent 12.6% of the population.

### Crude mortality rate

*   For every 100,000 Black Americans, about 379 have died from the coronavirus. This is about double the rate of Asian Americans, who have had the lowest rate, and around 25% less than Indigenous Americans, who have the highest rate.

*   In 37 states and Washington, D.C., more than 1 in 500 Black residents have died (i.e., more than 200 per 100,000).

### Age-adjusted mortality rate

*   Nationwide, the age-adjusted mortality rate for Black Americans (493 per 100,000) is about 2.2 times that of the group with the lowest age-adjusted mortality rate, which is Asian Americans (228 per 100,000).

*   Adjusting for age highlights a disparity in deaths between white and Black Americans in particular — the two groups have similar crude mortality rates, but the Black American age-adjusted mortality rate is around 55% higher than the same measure for white Americans.

*   Once adjusted for age, the highest COVID-19 mortality rates for Black Americans are in Mississippi (652), Iowa (636), Oklahoma (611), Nevada (610) and New Jersey (600).

Note: Nationwide statistics are derived from CDC reporting at the national level and are not suppressed. State level statistics are suppressed by CDC when the number of deaths is between 1-9.

*   In 46 states, more than 1 in 500 white residents have died (i.e., more than 200 per 100,000).

### Age-adjusted mortality rate

*   Nationwide, white Americans are the only group with an age-adjusted COVID-19 mortality rate (315 per 100,000) that is lower than the crude rate (386). Adjusting for age brings the mortality rate for white Americans from the second-highest to the second-lowest.

*   Once adjusted for age, the highest COVID-19 mortality rates for white Americans are in Kentucky (466), Mississippi (466), Oklahoma (454), Tennessee (437) and West Virginia (411).

Note: Nationwide statistics are derived from CDC reporting at the national level and are not suppressed. State level statistics are suppressed by CDC when the number of deaths is between 1-9.

* * *

_Editors note: This is a re-launched version of our_[_original Color of Coronavirus project_](https://www.apmresearchlab.org/covid/deaths-by-race-03-05-21)_, which ran from April 2020 through March 2021. That project was based on harvesting data from the COVID-19 statistics reported separately from each state. Since that time the CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics has developed a more robust system of tracking_[_COVID-19 mortality_](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/covid19/mortality-overview.htm)_, based on death certificates. While not without some issues (especially a known undercounting of American Indian deaths, which we address below) this data set is even more comprehensive than was the case in our original reporting of these issues. Even as we regret that tracking COVID-19 deaths is still a relevant pursuit, we hope that you will find our work meaningful and helpful in addressing the pandemic and understanding its impacts. As always, we welcome your feedback and insights (info@apmresearchlab.org)._

* * *

##### SOURCES

###### **Mortality Data**  
*   For total counts and for calculating cumulative crude rates and age-adjusted rates: [CDC/NCHS - Distribution of COVID-19 Deaths and Populations, by Jurisdiction, Age, and Race and Hispanic Origin](https://data.cdc.gov/NCHS/Distribution-of-COVID-19-Deaths-and-Populations-by/jwta-jxbg).
*   For counts over time and for crude rates over time, monthly/national: [CDC/NCHS - Provisional COVID-19 Deaths: Distribution of Deaths by Race and Hispanic Origin](https://data.cdc.gov/NCHS/Provisional-COVID-19-Deaths-Distribution-of-Deaths/pj7m-y5uh).
*   For counts over time and for crude rates over time quarterly/states: [CDC/NCHS - AH Quarterly Excess Deaths by State, Sex, Age, and Race](https://data.cdc.gov/NCHS/AH-Quarterly-Excess-Deaths-by-State-Sex-Age-and-Ra/jqg8-ycmh).
 According to the CDC, about 91% of these deaths have COVID-19 indicated as the underlying cause of death, while for the other 9% COVID-19 is one of multiple causes of death.  
  
**Population Data**  
 Mid-Year 2020 U.S. Census Data accessed via CDC-WONDER  
*   [National populations by race, all ages combined.](https://wonder.cdc.gov/controller/saved/D170/D278F683)
*   [State-level populations by race, all ages combined.](https://wonder.cdc.gov/controller/saved/D170/D279F330)
*   For age adjustment, national population by age groups: [Non-Hispanic](https://wonder.cdc.gov/controller/saved/D170/D279F896), [Hispanic](https://wonder.cdc.gov/controller/saved/D170/D279F900).
*   For age adjustment, state populations by age groups: [Non-Hispanic](https://wonder.cdc.gov/controller/saved/D170/D279F915), [Hispanic](https://wonder.cdc.gov/controller/saved/D170/D279F916).
  
 All calculations and subsequent analysis are by APM Research Lab and available on our [GitHub](https://github.com/APM-Research-Lab).

##### NOTES

###### **Racial and Ethnic Groups**  
Our labels of each racial or ethnic group correspond as follows: *   Latino — Hispanic or Latino ethnicity of any race
*   Pacific Islander — Non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander
*   Indigenous — Non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native
*   White — Non-Hispanic white
*   Black — Non-Hispanic Black or African American 
*   Asian — Non-Hispanic Asian 
*   More than one race — Non-Hispanic more than one race

###### As noted above, Indigenous American deaths [are known](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr70/NVSR70-12.pdf) to be underreported by 34%. [According to the CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/vsrr/covid19/tech_notes.htm), deaths are also known to be underreported for non-Hispanic API (3%) and for Hispanic decedents (3%).

###### Some CDC datasets include a "more than one race" racial category and some include an "other" category. We have included the data that indicates more than one race when available, for which there is also an overall population figure available as a denominator when calculating rates. No such denominator is available for calculating rates for the "other" category. The deaths listed in the "other" category constitute less than 1% of total reported deaths.

###### **Age-Adjusted Rates**  
 While there are many features of the novel coronavirus that are still unclear, this we know with certainty: The risk of dying from COVID-19 rises sharply with advanced age. [According to the CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/covid-data/investigations-discovery/hospitalization-death-by-age.html), people 65-74 years old have 65 times the risk of dying from COVID-19 compared to people aged 18-29. That risk increases to 140 times higher for people in the 75-84 age bracket, and 340 times for people age 85 or older.   
  
 Due to this steep age gradient to COVID-19 mortality, it is important to consider the varying age distributions of America's racial and ethnic groups. A higher share of white Americans are in the older age brackets than any other group. And even within the same race groups, the age distribution varies by location—with retirement destination states such as Florida having a much higher share of older adults within their white population, for example.   
  
 To remove the role of these age differences from COVID-19 mortality rates, we have also produced age-adjusted rates. There are two main categories of methods used to produce age-adjusted rates: direct and indirect standardization. The direct method uses the age distribution of COVID-19 deaths within a racial or ethnic group, while the indirect method takes the total number of COVID-19 deaths within a racial ethnic group and applies mortality rates by age group from the national level (all races) to the age distribution of that racial or ethnic group.   
  
 We have used the direct method where possible, but the direct method requires knowing the numbers of deaths for each age grouping for each race and, when calculating at the state level, for each state. For states with smaller populations, there are instances where not all of the age groupings reach the threshold of at least 10 to be released by CDC. For these suppressed groups/places, we have used the indirect method to calculate an age-adjusted rate.   
  
 To evaluate the accuracy of the indirectly age-adjusted rates, we compared direct and indirect rates where possible. Most indirect rates were within 5% of the direct rates. Some were up to 10% different and two were approaching 15% different. The higher errors tended to be for groups/places with lower numbers of COVID-19 deaths. For this reason, we chose to not calculate indirect rates for groups/places with fewer than 200 COVID-19 deaths. The indirect rates tended to be higher than the direct rates, but not universally.   
  
 All of these numbers are available for download on our [GitHub](https://github.com/APM-Research-Lab), including an indication of whether the age-adjustment for a particular group/place has been directly or indirectly calculated.   
  
 What do the results of these calculations mean? The age-adjusted rates indicate that many younger Americans who are Black, Latino, Indigenous or Pacific Islanders are dying of COVID-19—driving their mortality rates far above that of white and Asian Americans. Despite their relative youthfulness (a protective factor against COVID), their death rates are elevated.   
  
 It is important to note that, while age-adjusted mortality rates help us remove the influence of age differences in racial groups to examine disparities in outcomes, they are not the actual mortality rates experienced by these groups.
