![Image 3: COVID-ICU-ROSE-MEDICAL-CENTER-HOPE-201113](https://www.cpr.org/cdn-cgi/image/width=3840,quality=75,format=auto/https://wp-cpr.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2020/11/201113-COVID-ICU-ROSE-0011.jpg)

Hart Van Denburg/CPR News

Anna Hoppe, an RN at the Rose Medical Center COVID-19 intensive care unit, peers through a glass wall to check a patient, Nov. 13, 2020.

As of March 22, 2023, 15,007 Coloradans have now died in the coronavirus pandemic.

Colorado's [first COVID-19 death](https://www.cpr.org/2020/03/13/colorados-first-coronavirus-death-is-an-el-paso-county-woman-in-her-80s/) was an El Paso County woman in her 80s who died in a Colorado Springs hospital on March 13, 2020.

Since then, the pandemic has claimed enough people to fill [Red Rocks Amphitheatre](https://www.redrocksonline.com/our-story/history/) one and a half times.

“Fifteen thousand deaths is just terrible and it kind of forces us to reflect on what's happened,” said Dr. Anuj Mehta, a pulmonary care physician at Denver Health, and member of the [Colorado Vaccine Equity Taskforce](https://www.coloradovaccineequity.org/).

Reaching this milestone puts other changes in perspective.

“COVID has done so much more than just killed people. It's impacted people's lives,” Mehta said. That includes children who lost a parent or grandparent, those suffering from [long COVID](https://www.cpr.org/2022/12/08/colorado-long-covid-research/) and the other social and economic ripple effects of a global pandemic.

The 15,000 death mark is a loss of historic proportions, costing more lives than anything that’s happened in Colorado in 100 years. The magnitude of that is clearly seen in life expectancy rates in Colorado as the pandemic trimmed years off that bedrock measure of population health.

More often than not those who died were older and men. The virus devastated the Latino community perhaps more than any other ethnic group. It hit counties like Pueblo, Adams and El Paso harder than others.

Vaccination rates and other factors like comorbidities also are thought to have driven the broader trends. More than [seven out of 10 of all Coloradans got vaccinated](https://covid19.colorado.gov/vaccine-data-dashboard) with at least two COVID-19 vaccine doses. That, along with improved treatments and care, undoubtedly mitigated the pandemic’s reach.

“It doesn't take away from those that we lost for sure,” said Dr. Michelle Barron, an infectious disease expert at UCHealth. “But it could have been so much worse if we didn't have the tools that we had.”

Information about the deaths and other impacts caused by COVID-19, including from the state’s [COVID-19 dashboard](https://covid19.colorado.gov/data), posted by the Colorado Department of Health and Environment, reveals some telling details about the lives lost.

### More Coloradans have died due to COVID-19 than any historic event in the last century

The number of Coloradans who have died from COVID-19 is more than those killed in U.S. wars in the last century, and the 1918 influenza pandemic, combined.

The earlier pandemic claimed more than 7,500 lives at a time when the state’s population was much smaller, nearly [a million people](https://www.coloradovirtuallibrary.org/resource-sharing/state-pubs-blog/1918-influenza/#:~:text=In%20total%2C%20over%2049%2C000%20Coloradans,up%20quarantines%20in%20fraternity%20houses.).

* * *

* * *

So on a per capita basis the earlier pandemic caused a far greater relative loss of life, since the state now has nearly [6 million residents](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/CO), according to the U.S. Census.

Colorado became [a state in 1876](https://www.historycolorado.org/story/seasonal/2018/07/20/11-things-you-didnt-know-about-colorados-path-statehood), so it was not yet a state when the Civil War occurred in the prior decade.

### COVID-19 devastated Colorado’s oldest generation

Of the people who have died from COVID-19, around 14,000, the vast majority, were older than 50. The virus rocked the state’s oldest population, with more than 4,200 people over 85 years old falling to the disease.

And the number surely could have been higher, health experts say, if not for older Coloradans getting the vaccine at a high rate.

* * *

* * *

Virtually everyone in Colorado older than 65 — 99.9 percent — has completed the two-dose primary vaccine series.

But that number lags when it comes to the additional dose targeting the omicron variant, which became available in the fall of 2022. Slightly less than half of those older than 65 have received that booster dose.

According to CDC, advancing age is one of the [most consistent risk factors](https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/covid-data/investigations-discovery/hospitalization-death-by-age.html) for severe COVID-19 outcomes. Adults 85 years and older are 15 times more likely to be hospitalized with COVID and [350 times more likely to die](https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/covid-data/investigations-discovery/hospitalization-death-by-age.html#:~:text=Sample%20interpretation%3A%20Compared%20with%20ages,to%2029%20years%20age%20group.)) of the disease compared to adults aged 18-29 years.

### El Paso County lost the most people, but among large counties, Adams and Pueblo counties saw higher death rates

Not surprisingly, the bulk of the Coloradans who lost their lives to the virus lived in more urban areas, along the Front Range. But some counties did much worse than others, according to the [state dashboard](https://covid19.colorado.gov/data) and other available data.

[Studies](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9015592/), conducted both [nationally](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/72/wr/mm7206a3.htm?s_cid=mm7206a3_w) and [internationally](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lanam/article/PIIS2667-193X(22)00008-4/fulltext), consistently find locations with higher rates of vaccination have lower rates of death from COVID, according to the state health department.

El Paso County lost more lives to COVID than any other, more than 2,200. That is more than 15 percent of the total deaths, greater than that county’s share of the state’s population.

* * *

* * *

Adams, Jefferson, Arapahoe and Denver counties all documented more than a thousand deaths.

Another group of large Front Range counties all recorded more than 650 deaths: Pueblo, Larimer, Boulder, Mesa, Douglas and Weld.

Pueblo and Adams had by far the highest death rates, among the state’s largest counties, according to the [NYTimes](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2021/us/colorado-covid-cases.html).

Pueblo County’s rate was 411 per 100,000 residents based on age-adjusted COVID-19 death rates. It had the lowest vaccination rate among the ten biggest Colorado counties.

The second highest death rate among those counties was in Adams County, with 332 per 100,000 residents.

The state’s age-adjusted COVID-19 death rate was 240 per 100,000K residents. Of the 15 counties with more than 55,000 people, Eagle County had the lowest death rate of 72 per 100,000 residents. Of that group, Eagle is the most vaccinated county with 91 percent of its 18+ population fully vaccinated, well above the state’s 81 percent average, according to the state health department.

Boulder County also had a relatively lower death rate at 132 per 100,000, as well as higher two-dose vaccination rate at 85 percent. The same was true for Broomfield County with a death rate of 176 per 100,000 and 88 percent of its population older than 18 fully vaccinated with two doses.

More than 30 counties, many medium or small-sized, suffered fewer than 200 lives lost to the virus.

Nearly 20 counties, mostly sparsely populated, many on the Eastern Plains, did not record a single COVID-19 death.

### Colorado’s Latino community was hit disproportionately hard

Coronavirus was the top cause of death among Hispanics, as well as non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian, Other Pacific Islanders and American Indian/Native Alaskans, according to state life expectancy data released in 2022.

“COVID mortality is really a reflection of underlying disparities in health,” said Dr. Rocio Pereira. She directs the Office of Health Equity at Denver Health. “It's not a surprise really that we're seeing these numbers.”

Two counties with large Hispanic populations, Pueblo ([44 percent Hispanic](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/pueblocountycolorado), according to the U.S Census), and Adams ([42 percent](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/adamscountycolorado)) had by far the highest death rates among the state’s large counties.

* * *

* * *

The relatively low vaccination rate for Hispanic Coloradans is helping to drive the trend, according to Julissa Soto, an independent health equity consultant, who works with nonprofits in Colorado and nationally.

CDPHE reports almost [50 percent of Colorado Hispanics](https://covid19.colorado.gov/vaccine-data-dashboard) have had at least one COVID-19 dose. That compares with 86 percent of non-Hispanic whites.

“The pandemic emergency is fading out for some, but the emergency in health access for Latinos remains,” Soto said. “Much more needs to be done to address health inequity in Colorado.”

This population often has less access to basic health care, said Pereira, like a primary care doctor, where they can discuss and get access to vaccines. Many live in multigenerational housing.

“This population also has high exposure to the virus,” she said. “They work in service industries where they are more likely to be interacting with people. They didn't have the luxury of working from home or taking time off.”

They have higher comorbidities, the condition of having two or more diseases at the same time, Pereira said, things like obesity, diabetes and lung disease. That’s made them more vulnerable to COVID-19.

The state’s [data on COVID-19 deaths](https://covid19.colorado.gov/data) by race and ethnicity, according to CDC provisional data, have been wildly inconsistent in recent weeks. Last month, a graph on the state’s website showed that 4,600 of the total deaths were Hispanic. That’s almost 26 percent of the state’s total deaths, more than that demographic’s 22 percent share of the state population.

In mid-March, the same graph had changed to show Hispanics making up far fewer deaths at 3,445.

According to an agency spokesperson, CDPHE found an issue with how it tabulated data for the CDC last week. The [CDC groups data](https://data.cdc.gov/NCHS/Provisional-COVID-19-Deaths-by-Race-and-Hispanic-O/ks3g-spdg) into overlapping age groups. When CDPHE displayed that on its webpage in the race and ethnicity demographic, some deaths were counted twice. The data on the visualization are now correct, the spokesperson said.

Despite the recent changes and issues in the data, “I think there's no question these disparities exist,” said Denver Health’s Mehta. “I can speak to that very personally. Not only at my hospital, but hospitals where my colleagues work, we've seen patients who identify as Hispanic being a much larger proportion of the severe cases than other groups.”

That dovetails with national research. [An analysis released this month by the Kaiser Family Foundation](https://www.kff.org/racial-equity-and-health-policy/report/key-data-on-health-and-health-care-by-race-and-ethnicity/) found that Black, Hispanic and American Indian and Alaska Native people fared worse than white people across the majority of examined measures of health, health care and social determinants of health.

### More men than women died from COVID-19

Nearly 56 percent of those who died were men, compared with 44 percent women, according to the [state’s dashboard](https://covid19.colorado.gov/data).

Vaccination status may play a role in the difference.

By sex, more than 80 percent of Colorado women have received at least one dose of the COVID-19 vaccine, according to the state’s [vaccine dashboard](https://covid19.colorado.gov/vaccine-data-dashboard). For Colorado men, the rate was about 5 percent lower, at about 75 percent.

Not surprisingly, a large gap also exists between the genders regarding booster shots, with about 54 percent of Colorado women having gotten the additional dose, compared with 46 percent of men.

A higher mortality rate among men has been consistently observed throughout the pandemic in global and national data, with larger gaps than seen in Colorado, according to the state health department.

### Coloradans have lost years of life expectancy during the pandemic

Last year, the state health department reported that in 2021, for the second consecutive year, the [life expectancy of Colorado residents fell](https://www.cpr.org/2022/06/25/colorado-life-expectancy-falls-covid-overdose-deaths/). Data is not yet available for 2022.

Life expectancy dropped to 78 years in 2021. That's a bit lower than the 78.4 years reported for 2020, which was the first year of the pandemic. But the state figures showed the decline represented a [persistent and significant drop](https://www.cpr.org/2021/06/25/pandemic-life-expectancy-fell-health-care-inequality/) of nearly three years compared to 2019.

The trend is of historic proportion.

“The last time life expectancy dropped like this was in 1943, which was the most fatal year of World War II, for the nation,” Dr. Eric France, the state’s chief medical officer told CPR last year. “It is tragic that we see life expectancy drop. Death rates increased by 20 percent.”

Driving the troubling numbers were both the COVID-19 virus and overdose deaths.

COVID-19 remained the third leading cause of death among Colorado residents in 2021, as it was in 2020, the health department found.

Some demographic groups in particular were hard hit. Coronavirus was the top cause of death among Hispanics, as well as non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islanders and American Indian/Native Alaskans, according to the state’s data.

# 15,000 Coloradans have died due to COVID, a loss of historic proportions

![Image 2](https://www.cpr.org/cdn-cgi/image/width=3840,quality=75,format=auto/https://wp-cpr.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2019/05/2014.cpr-staff-john_daley-square-for-web.creditcpr.jpg)

Hart Van Denburg/CPR News

Anna Hoppe, an RN at the Rose Medical Center COVID-19 intensive care unit, peers through a glass wall to check a patient, Nov. 13, 2020.

As of March 22, 2023, 15,007 Coloradans have now died in the coronavirus pandemic.

Colorado's [first COVID-19 death](https://www.cpr.org/2020/03/13/colorados-first-coronavirus-death-is-an-el-paso-county-woman-in-her-80s/) was an El Paso County woman in her 80s who died in a Colorado Springs hospital on March 13, 2020.

Since then, the pandemic has claimed enough people to fill [Red Rocks Amphitheatre](https://www.redrocksonline.com/our-story/history/) one and a half times.

“Fifteen thousand deaths is just terrible and it kind of forces us to reflect on what's happened,” said Dr. Anuj Mehta, a pulmonary care physician at Denver Health, and member of the [Colorado Vaccine Equity Taskforce](https://www.coloradovaccineequity.org/).

Reaching this milestone puts other changes in perspective.

“COVID has done so much more than just killed people. It's impacted people's lives,” Mehta said. That includes children who lost a parent or grandparent, those suffering from [long COVID](https://www.cpr.org/2022/12/08/colorado-long-covid-research/) and the other social and economic ripple effects of a global pandemic.

The 15,000 death mark is a loss of historic proportions, costing more lives than anything that’s happened in Colorado in 100 years. The magnitude of that is clearly seen in life expectancy rates in Colorado as the pandemic trimmed years off that bedrock measure of population health.

More often than not those who died were older and men. The virus devastated the Latino community perhaps more than any other ethnic group. It hit counties like Pueblo, Adams and El Paso harder than others.

Vaccination rates and other factors like comorbidities also are thought to have driven the broader trends. More than [seven out of 10 of all Coloradans got vaccinated](https://covid19.colorado.gov/vaccine-data-dashboard) with at least two COVID-19 vaccine doses. That, along with improved treatments and care, undoubtedly mitigated the pandemic’s reach.

“It doesn't take away from those that we lost for sure,” said Dr. Michelle Barron, an infectious disease expert at UCHealth. “But it could have been so much worse if we didn't have the tools that we had.”

Information about the deaths and other impacts caused by COVID-19, including from the state’s [COVID-19 dashboard](https://covid19.colorado.gov/data), posted by the Colorado Department of Health and Environment, reveals some telling details about the lives lost.

### More Coloradans have died due to COVID-19 than any historic event in the last century

The number of Coloradans who have died from COVID-19 is more than those killed in U.S. wars in the last century, and the 1918 influenza pandemic, combined.

The earlier pandemic claimed more than 7,500 lives at a time when the state’s population was much smaller, nearly [a million people](https://www.coloradovirtuallibrary.org/resource-sharing/state-pubs-blog/1918-influenza/#:~:text=In%20total%2C%20over%2049%2C000%20Coloradans,up%20quarantines%20in%20fraternity%20houses.).

* * *

* * *

So on a per capita basis the earlier pandemic caused a far greater relative loss of life, since the state now has nearly [6 million residents](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/CO), according to the U.S. Census.

Colorado became [a state in 1876](https://www.historycolorado.org/story/seasonal/2018/07/20/11-things-you-didnt-know-about-colorados-path-statehood), so it was not yet a state when the Civil War occurred in the prior decade.

### COVID-19 devastated Colorado’s oldest generation

Of the people who have died from COVID-19, around 14,000, the vast majority, were older than 50. The virus rocked the state’s oldest population, with more than 4,200 people over 85 years old falling to the disease.

And the number surely could have been higher, health experts say, if not for older Coloradans getting the vaccine at a high rate.

* * *

* * *

Virtually everyone in Colorado older than 65 — 99.9 percent — has completed the two-dose primary vaccine series.

But that number lags when it comes to the additional dose targeting the omicron variant, which became available in the fall of 2022. Slightly less than half of those older than 65 have received that booster dose.

According to CDC, advancing age is one of the [most consistent risk factors](https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/covid-data/investigations-discovery/hospitalization-death-by-age.html) for severe COVID-19 outcomes. Adults 85 years and older are 15 times more likely to be hospitalized with COVID and [350 times more likely to die](https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/covid-data/investigations-discovery/hospitalization-death-by-age.html#:~:text=Sample%20interpretation%3A%20Compared%20with%20ages,to%2029%20years%20age%20group.)) of the disease compared to adults aged 18-29 years.

### El Paso County lost the most people, but among large counties, Adams and Pueblo counties saw higher death rates

Not surprisingly, the bulk of the Coloradans who lost their lives to the virus lived in more urban areas, along the Front Range. But some counties did much worse than others, according to the [state dashboard](https://covid19.colorado.gov/data) and other available data.

[Studies](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9015592/), conducted both [nationally](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/72/wr/mm7206a3.htm?s_cid=mm7206a3_w) and [internationally](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lanam/article/PIIS2667-193X(22)00008-4/fulltext), consistently find locations with higher rates of vaccination have lower rates of death from COVID, according to the state health department.

El Paso County lost more lives to COVID than any other, more than 2,200. That is more than 15 percent of the total deaths, greater than that county’s share of the state’s population.

* * *

* * *

Adams, Jefferson, Arapahoe and Denver counties all documented more than a thousand deaths.

Another group of large Front Range counties all recorded more than 650 deaths: Pueblo, Larimer, Boulder, Mesa, Douglas and Weld.

Pueblo and Adams had by far the highest death rates, among the state’s largest counties, according to the [NYTimes](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2021/us/colorado-covid-cases.html).

Pueblo County’s rate was 411 per 100,000 residents based on age-adjusted COVID-19 death rates. It had the lowest vaccination rate among the ten biggest Colorado counties.

The second highest death rate among those counties was in Adams County, with 332 per 100,000 residents.

The state’s age-adjusted COVID-19 death rate was 240 per 100,000K residents. Of the 15 counties with more than 55,000 people, Eagle County had the lowest death rate of 72 per 100,000 residents. Of that group, Eagle is the most vaccinated county with 91 percent of its 18+ population fully vaccinated, well above the state’s 81 percent average, according to the state health department.

Boulder County also had a relatively lower death rate at 132 per 100,000, as well as higher two-dose vaccination rate at 85 percent. The same was true for Broomfield County with a death rate of 176 per 100,000 and 88 percent of its population older than 18 fully vaccinated with two doses.

More than 30 counties, many medium or small-sized, suffered fewer than 200 lives lost to the virus.

Nearly 20 counties, mostly sparsely populated, many on the Eastern Plains, did not record a single COVID-19 death.

### Colorado’s Latino community was hit disproportionately hard

Coronavirus was the top cause of death among Hispanics, as well as non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian, Other Pacific Islanders and American Indian/Native Alaskans, according to state life expectancy data released in 2022.

“COVID mortality is really a reflection of underlying disparities in health,” said Dr. Rocio Pereira. She directs the Office of Health Equity at Denver Health. “It's not a surprise really that we're seeing these numbers.”

Two counties with large Hispanic populations, Pueblo ([44 percent Hispanic](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/pueblocountycolorado), according to the U.S Census), and Adams ([42 percent](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/adamscountycolorado)) had by far the highest death rates among the state’s large counties.

* * *

* * *

The relatively low vaccination rate for Hispanic Coloradans is helping to drive the trend, according to Julissa Soto, an independent health equity consultant, who works with nonprofits in Colorado and nationally.

CDPHE reports almost [50 percent of Colorado Hispanics](https://covid19.colorado.gov/vaccine-data-dashboard) have had at least one COVID-19 dose. That compares with 86 percent of non-Hispanic whites.

“The pandemic emergency is fading out for some, but the emergency in health access for Latinos remains,” Soto said. “Much more needs to be done to address health inequity in Colorado.”

This population often has less access to basic health care, said Pereira, like a primary care doctor, where they can discuss and get access to vaccines. Many live in multigenerational housing.

“This population also has high exposure to the virus,” she said. “They work in service industries where they are more likely to be interacting with people. They didn't have the luxury of working from home or taking time off.”

They have higher comorbidities, the condition of having two or more diseases at the same time, Pereira said, things like obesity, diabetes and lung disease. That’s made them more vulnerable to COVID-19.

The state’s [data on COVID-19 deaths](https://covid19.colorado.gov/data) by race and ethnicity, according to CDC provisional data, have been wildly inconsistent in recent weeks. Last month, a graph on the state’s website showed that 4,600 of the total deaths were Hispanic. That’s almost 26 percent of the state’s total deaths, more than that demographic’s 22 percent share of the state population.

In mid-March, the same graph had changed to show Hispanics making up far fewer deaths at 3,445.

According to an agency spokesperson, CDPHE found an issue with how it tabulated data for the CDC last week. The [CDC groups data](https://data.cdc.gov/NCHS/Provisional-COVID-19-Deaths-by-Race-and-Hispanic-O/ks3g-spdg) into overlapping age groups. When CDPHE displayed that on its webpage in the race and ethnicity demographic, some deaths were counted twice. The data on the visualization are now correct, the spokesperson said.

Despite the recent changes and issues in the data, “I think there's no question these disparities exist,” said Denver Health’s Mehta. “I can speak to that very personally. Not only at my hospital, but hospitals where my colleagues work, we've seen patients who identify as Hispanic being a much larger proportion of the severe cases than other groups.”

That dovetails with national research. [An analysis released this month by the Kaiser Family Foundation](https://www.kff.org/racial-equity-and-health-policy/report/key-data-on-health-and-health-care-by-race-and-ethnicity/) found that Black, Hispanic and American Indian and Alaska Native people fared worse than white people across the majority of examined measures of health, health care and social determinants of health.

### More men than women died from COVID-19

Nearly 56 percent of those who died were men, compared with 44 percent women, according to the [state’s dashboard](https://covid19.colorado.gov/data).

Vaccination status may play a role in the difference.

By sex, more than 80 percent of Colorado women have received at least one dose of the COVID-19 vaccine, according to the state’s [vaccine dashboard](https://covid19.colorado.gov/vaccine-data-dashboard). For Colorado men, the rate was about 5 percent lower, at about 75 percent.

Not surprisingly, a large gap also exists between the genders regarding booster shots, with about 54 percent of Colorado women having gotten the additional dose, compared with 46 percent of men.

A higher mortality rate among men has been consistently observed throughout the pandemic in global and national data, with larger gaps than seen in Colorado, according to the state health department.

### Coloradans have lost years of life expectancy during the pandemic

Last year, the state health department reported that in 2021, for the second consecutive year, the [life expectancy of Colorado residents fell](https://www.cpr.org/2022/06/25/colorado-life-expectancy-falls-covid-overdose-deaths/). Data is not yet available for 2022.

Life expectancy dropped to 78 years in 2021. That's a bit lower than the 78.4 years reported for 2020, which was the first year of the pandemic. But the state figures showed the decline represented a [persistent and significant drop](https://www.cpr.org/2021/06/25/pandemic-life-expectancy-fell-health-care-inequality/) of nearly three years compared to 2019.

The trend is of historic proportion.

“The last time life expectancy dropped like this was in 1943, which was the most fatal year of World War II, for the nation,” Dr. Eric France, the state’s chief medical officer told CPR last year. “It is tragic that we see life expectancy drop. Death rates increased by 20 percent.”

Driving the troubling numbers were both the COVID-19 virus and overdose deaths.

COVID-19 remained the third leading cause of death among Colorado residents in 2021, as it was in 2020, the health department found.

Some demographic groups in particular were hard hit. Coronavirus was the top cause of death among Hispanics, as well as non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islanders and American Indian/Native Alaskans, according to the state’s data.

## Abstract

### Context:

The Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic occurred during a time of political tension in the United States. County-level political environment may have been influential in COVID-19 outcomes.

### Objective:

This study examined the association between county-level political environment and age-adjusted COVID-19 mortality rates from 2020 to 2022.

### Design & Setting:

Political environment was measured by the 2020 Presidential election results and compared with age-adjusted COVID-19 mortality rates by county in Colorado.

### Main Outcome Measures:

Rate ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were estimated using negative binomial regression incorporating a population offset term. Models adjusted for populational differences using the demographics percentile from Colorado’s EnviroScreen Environmental Justice Tool.

### Results:

Age-adjusted county mortality rates ranged from 14.3 to 446.8.0 per 100 000. 2021 COVID-19 mortality rates were nearly twice as high in counties voting for Donald Trump compared to those voting for Joseph Biden (adjusted RR=1.98, 95% CI: 1.59, 2.47). Results for 2020 and 2022 mortality models were also in the positive direction, though the confidence intervals crossed null values.

### Conclusion:

These results build on a growing body of evidence that political environment may have been influential for COVID-19 mortality, helping to understand the drivers of health outcomes. Implications for the public health system as we shift into the endemic period of COVID-19 include motivation for collaborative work to restore and rebuild trust among and between stakeholders and the community, as well as increase health education given its’ influence on both individual and community behaviors.

**Keywords:**COVID-19, mortality, politics, public health

## Methods

### Study population

In order to assess county-level associations between age-adjusted COVID-19 mortality rates and 2016 & 2020 Presidential election voting results within the state of Colorado, we selected an ecologic study design. There are a total of 64 counties in the state of Colorado. Inclusion in the study was based on availability of COVID-19 mortality data for each county in a given year. Mortality data from 48 Colorado counties were available for 2020, data from 56 counties were available for 2021, and data from 49 counties were available for 2022. We selected county level analysis as we hypothesize that within the context of a respiratory pathogen, exposure and risk may be defined by the health behaviors of those in the surrounding community in addition to the choices made by individuals. As discussed in the introduction, county-level decisions also became critical during the pandemic.

### Exposure of interest

Utilizing data from the Colorado Secretary of State, a binary exposure variable was constructed as an indicator of the voting outcome in each county in the 2020 Presidential election. Counties that Trump won were assigned the exposure, while counties Joseph Biden won were considered unexposed. Every county in the state voted in highest percentage for one of those candidates during the election, and as such, there were no additional candidates to use in this comparison.23,24

### Outcomes of interest

The outcomes of interest were the age-adjusted annual COVID-19 mortality rates in 2020, 2021, and 2022. International Classification of Disease, 10th edition (ICD-10) Code U07.1 was used as the identification criterion for death certificates, indicating cases where COVID-19 was listed as the primary or underlying cause of death. Mortality data were obtained from the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (CDPHE). Under CDPHE suppression rules, data for counties with 2 or fewer deaths in a given calendar year were unavailable, which primarily impacted counties with small populations. CDPHE used the 2000 United States Census to calculate the age-adjusted rates based on the counts using standardization.

### Covariate

To account for potential confounding resulting from county level differences in demographic variables, we selected the demographics percentile from the Colorado EnviroScreen Environmental Justice tool for use in adjusted models.25 Colorado EnviroScreen is an interactive environmental justice mapping tool created by CDPHE that uses data from 35 different metrics to construct scores used to compare the overall burden from 1 county to the next within the state. There is an overall score available for each county as well as sub-scores for groups of components. The demographics percentile metric was chosen for inclusion in this study because it incorporates information on county-level income, disability, language, housing burden, race, and ethnicity, allowing for efficient adjustment for multiple variations in population and socio-economic factors simultaneously. (More description of Colorado EnviroScreen methodology is available in the Supplemental materials.)25

### Statistical analysis

Due to overdispersion in the mortality data, negative binomial regression models were selected and constructed separately for each year of outcome data (2020, 2021, and 2022), regressed against the binary indicator for election outcome in 2020, resulting in a total of 3 exposure/outcome models for the analysis. In addition to the binary exposure variable, all models were adjusted using the demographics percentile from Colorado EnviroScreen and included a population offset term to account for the wide variation in county level population. The offset term was calculated using the CDPHE provided age-adjusted mortality rate multiplied times the provided annual population in each county, then divided by 100 000. The resulting value is an age-adjusted count for deaths in each county, which is then modeled with an offset based on the total population in that county. Models with a population offset term were selected as primary due to better model fit a measured by AIC and BIC compared to models without the offset term.

As a sensitivity analysis and in comparison to the negative binomial results, adjusted models were built using Quasi-Poisson regression, again including a population offset term. Negative binomial and Quasi-Poisson regression methods are both appropriate for use in situations where overdispersion is present in the data, as was the case regarding the COVID-19 mortality outcome data.26

We recognize that use of 2020 election data may introduce concerns regarding temporality, as most of the year had already occurred, including 8 months of the pandemic, at the time of the election, and it is possible that the pandemic itself had influence on the outcome of that election. In consideration of this reality, models using 2016 election data for the exposure instead of 2020 were constructed for a second sensitivity analysis, and the correlation between 2016 and 2020 election data was assessed using a Spearman test.

Finally, a third sensitivity analysis used a continuous vote percentage as the exposure rather than a binary indicator, modeled for a 10% increase in the vote for Trump, adjusting for demographics.

Statistical analyses were primarily performed in R, version 4.3.1, with some preliminary data cleaning conducted using Microsoft Excel. The present study was reviewed by the University Institutional Review Board, Biomedical Division and deemed not to be human subjects research. Protocol 4034, determination date December 1, 2022. The datasets generated and analyzed for the current study are available in Dryad Data Repository, DOI: 10.5061/dryad.573n5tbfh.

## Results

In the 2020 Presidential election, Trump won 40 counties in Colorado, while Biden won 24. Although Trump won more counties, the mean county population was over 3 times higher in counties that Biden won than in counties that Trump won. Mean mortality values for counties Trump won were higher than in counties Biden won for all years of the outcome data. Age-adjusted county-level annual COVID-19 mortality rates over the 3-year study period ranged from 14.3 to 446.8 per 100 000, with the highest rates occurring in 2021. The first sensitivity analysis used adjusted Quasi-Poisson models with a population offset, which again yielded statistically significant findings for 2021 mortality, though attenuated from the negative binomial model results. Although point estimates indicated a slightly negative association for 2020 and a slightly positive association for 2022 data, confidence intervals for both years included the null. Regarding the choice of election data, our second sensitivity analysis compared years of election data. A Spearman test comparing the 2 years of election data was found to have a positive correlation of 0.87, with 62 degrees of freedom, and a corresponding _P_ value of<.001, indicating there was a high level of agreement between the 2 elections. In 4 counties, election results shifted parties between parties in the 2016 and 2020 elections, with 3 moving from the Republican party candidate, Trump, to the Democratic party candidate, Biden, and 1 moving in the opposite direction. In comparison with 2020 election models, regression models using 2016 election data instead of 2020 election data yielded similar findings with very slightly attenuated estimates. Finally, modeling election data as a continuous variable in our third sensitivity analysis instead of a binary variable resulted in positive, statistically significant associations for all years. A 10% increase in the county-level vote percentage for Trump was found to be associated with between 13% and 21% increased COVID-19 mortality. (Continuous model results are available in Supplemental Table S4, available at [http://links.lww.com/JPHMP/B456](http://links.lww.com/JPHMP/B456)).

## Discussion

We found a statistically significant association between county-level political environment as measured by election results and age-adjusted COVID-19 mortality rates in 2021 which was robust to all methods of sensitivity analyses and adds to a growing body of evidence that political environment was associated with COVID-19 mortality in Colorado. In Colorado, counties voting for Trump experienced nearly twice the COVID-19 mortality rate in 2021. Significant results were not identified for COVID-19 mortality in the other years of the pandemic studied.

Variation in associations by year may be attributed to a number of factors. In the first year of the pandemic, politics appeared to impact mitigation measures, social distancing, mask mandates, closures, and remote schooling decisions.7 In this early stage, it is possible that COVID-19 mortality data are not accurate due to lack of available tests and inconsistent reporting.16 Further in the second and third year of the pandemic, the influence of political ideation appeared to be primarily concerned with influencing vaccination status. The relationship between county level vaccination rates and mortality has been demonstrated.27 A possible explanation for the nonsignificant findings in 2022 mortality may be related to the depletion of susceptibles both in terms of vaccination status and mortality from the virus.28,29 As time progressed, there were fewer and fewer unvaccinated people and those most vulnerable might have already succumbed to the virus.

The relationship between political environment and COVID-19 mortality appears to be mediated by vaccination. In essence this means that vaccination is on a causal pathway between the 2, explaining at least some of the association. This relationship is supported by the 2023 findings of Alemi and Lee, who studied the mediation effect for vaccines in COVID-19.30 Given the likely role of vaccination as a mediator, vaccination rates were not included separately as a predictor in the model because doing so would block the portion of the association on that mediated pathway. (A directed acyclic graph is included in the Supplemental Materials, Figure S1, available at [http://links.lww.com/JPHMP/B456](http://links.lww.com/JPHMP/B456), demonstrating included variables and the vaccine mediated pathway).

Election data are only made available aggregated by geography, the smallest unit of which is the county level in Colorado. Individual level data are not available and can only be estimated through reliance on polls. Although sometimes used to measure political environment, party affiliation was not selected as the exposure for this study with intention given that a high percentage of unaffiliated voters are registered in Colorado. Laws in the state allow unaffiliated individuals to vote in primaries, reducing the need to choose a formal affiliation.31,32 Because county-level officials hold office in a non-partisan fashion in Colorado, there is no way to assess the connection between their decisions related to mitigation, education, vaccination promotion and their political affiliations. In light of the above considerations, we determined that aggregated presidential vote data were an appropriate proxy for political environment at the county level.

We analyzed the association here using both 2016 and 2020 election data with intention to capture how, if at all, these relationships may have differed. Correlation results indicated a high level of agreement between the election data; however, these data are not fully correlated. Creating separate models for each year of election data allowed determination of whether those small differences in the election data year to year resulted in meaningful changes to the association with COVID-19 mortality. If only 2016 election data were utilized, results may not have captured the full impact of the county-level political environment closer to the outcome years under study. Likewise, using only the 2020 election data might have created the above mentioned temporality concerns. The choice here to include both years provides broader information for the exploration of these associations, and overall, primary models built using the 2020 election exposure tended to have slightly stronger point estimates than sensitivity models using the 2016 election exposure, though the findings were largely in agreement.

Although the continuous models in the third sensitivity analysis provide valuable information about the connection between vote percentage and mortality, they were not selected as the primary models here because they are not tied to the actual election outcome for each county, reflecting only the linear relationship between the variables.

### Strengths of this study

Data were made available from CDPHE as age-adjusted rates, which automatically addresses the confounder of the populational age distribution at the county level. The use of the Colorado EnviroScreen demographics percentile as a covariate in this analysis is a strength. Although Colorado EnviroScreen was created for environmental justice applications for the community, agencies, and governmental institutions, this study demonstrates the utility of the composite demographics measures as a way to efficiently adjust for multiple county-level confounders at once in health research. Additional strengths of this study include state-wide analysis and the utilization of publicly available data sources. The agreement in the results using different modeling techniques, including those in the sensitivity analysis lend robustness to the findings and increases confidence in the associations found regarding 2021 COVID-19 mortality.

### Limitations of this study

Using an ecologic study, we are limited here in interpretation, knowing these findings cannot be extrapolated to the individual level. This analysis focused on the county level with intention due to our interest in the influence of community level exposures. Residual confounding for the variables included in the demographics score as well as unmeasured confounding are always a possibility. We hypothesize that it would be highly unlikely for any additional predictor to have a strong enough relationship to negate the associations found in this study. We recognize that people who live and work in different counties exist, which may result in some exposure misclassification, though any misclassification present as a result would most likely be nondifferential given that crossing county boundaries for work does not occur in a differential manner. In terms of selection bias, the exclusion of counties with missing data is not likely to be very influential in this study. Most counties representing a total of 98.4% of the overall state population were included in the analysis.

It is possible that use of ICD codes to determine COVID-19 mortality resulted in substantially undercounting actual deaths, potentially including the limitation of only counting patients where COVID-19 was listed as the underlying cause of death. Rural areas in Colorado are more likely to have coroners versus medical examiners, and it has been established that coroners are more likely to make errors in cause of death determinations.33 Coroners are frequently chosen through elections in Colorado and as such might have been open to influence from regional politics as a result.34 It is therefore possible that some misclassification of the outcome occurred here, and if so, there is a further possibility that misclassification would be differential. The directionality of this misclassification would lead us, perhaps, to an even stronger association. There is also a possibility that the number of deaths was even higher than documented in 2020 due to the evolving status of the COVID-19 pandemic and early lack of available tests. Some have argued that it might be a more accurate measure to utilize data on excess mortality rather than focus solely on deaths specifically coded for COVID-19 to more fully capture the mortality effects of the pandemic.35,36

In the present ecologic study, we cannot determine the influence of individual level political views or how those individual views may influence the county-wide environment because only aggregated election data were utilized here. Additionally, the specific findings of one study using voter registration data rather than election data found that individual political affiliation was associated with excess deaths during the COVID-19.19 The present research finds similar associations using actual election data rather than voter registration, perhaps adding some evidence of the similarity of both measures to describe community level political environment. Ideally, future research would look at the combined influence of both individual and community level political views on health outcomes, including COVID-19 specific mortality and excess mortality rates.

An additional limitation of this study is that our specific findings may not be generalizable to states outside of Colorado. Although the results here align with other similar studies,19,20 the characteristics of each state are unique in terms of population demographics and distribution, the political environment, and the nature of voter registration requirements. We believe that use of actual voting data is more directly relevant to research in Colorado because so many voters in Colorado are unaffiliated.

## Conclusion

This study finds an ecologic association between county-level political environment and COVID-19 mortality. As we move into the endemic period in COVID-19’s history, exploring the differences of COVID-19 mortality is necessary to inform future decisions. If political environment truly is associated with COVID-19 mortality, as our findings indicate, intentional work to restore and build faith and trust in the public health system is essential.37 There is a real opportunity here to learn from this experience and to address some of the most critical needs as we emerge from the COVID-19 pandemic. To best build the collaborative relationships necessary for a responsive and equitable public health system, we encourage open dialogue and engagement among policymakers, employers, public health agencies, health care groups, advocacy groups, and community partners about the drivers of health outcomes in the most transparent manner possible to allow for shared priority setting, coordination, education and planning.38 Working toward better collaboration between the medical care system and the public health system will better position us all for the next pandemic.39

This study provides an opportunity to learn from and to address some critical needs in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic that may support future public health infectious disease planning efforts. Given the realities of climate change and of living in a global economy, this likely will not be our last pandemic. Within the context of COVID-19 and other infectious disease, this carries implications for the importance of health education and mitigation strategies as well as vaccination approaches. If politics are indeed a predictor for health outcomes such as COVID-19 mortality, it is possible that this relationship between political environment and outcomes exists for more health conditions than we are aware, and additional study into the relationships between political environment and other health outcomes, both related to communicable and non-communicable diseases, should be pursued. Moving forward, perhaps the lesson here is that it may be beneficial for both researchers and public health practitioners to view political environment as a potential predictor of health outcomes in an effort to better assess risk, develop mitigation strategies as needed, and design meaningful communication, collaboration and education that are consistent across party lines.40 Implications for Policy & Practice The identification of political environment as a predictor of risk builds awareness of this factor’s influence on both individuals and communities and should provide motivation for robust, clear, and intentional health education and communication.As COVID-19 transitions toward endemicity and we confront the reality that this will not be our last pandemic, public health agencies and governmental institutions need to understand the relationship between politics and health outcomes; this study may foster the creation of unique opportunities for vital community liaisons and trusted messengers to help bridge communication gaps.This study’s findings urge cooperation and collaboration between community member and partners, researchers, public health agencies, governmental bodies, educational institutions, industry, media, and other stakeholders—and should inform interactions between these groups with the overarching goal of shared decision-making, informed by scientific methods and public health ethics principles.

## Abstract

### Context:

The Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic occurred during a time of political tension in the United States. County-level political environment may have been influential in COVID-19 outcomes.

### Objective:

This study examined the association between county-level political environment and age-adjusted COVID-19 mortality rates from 2020 to 2022.

### Design & Setting:

Political environment was measured by the 2020 Presidential election results and compared with age-adjusted COVID-19 mortality rates by county in Colorado.

### Main Outcome Measures:

Rate ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were estimated using negative binomial regression incorporating a population offset term. Models adjusted for populational differences using the demographics percentile from Colorado’s EnviroScreen Environmental Justice Tool.

### Results:

Age-adjusted county mortality rates ranged from 14.3 to 446.8.0 per 100 000. 2021 COVID-19 mortality rates were nearly twice as high in counties voting for Donald Trump compared to those voting for Joseph Biden (adjusted RR=1.98, 95% CI: 1.59, 2.47). Results for 2020 and 2022 mortality models were also in the positive direction, though the confidence intervals crossed null values.

### Conclusion:

These results build on a growing body of evidence that political environment may have been influential for COVID-19 mortality, helping to understand the drivers of health outcomes. Implications for the public health system as we shift into the endemic period of COVID-19 include motivation for collaborative work to restore and rebuild trust among and between stakeholders and the community, as well as increase health education given its’ influence on both individual and community behaviors.

**Keywords:**COVID-19, mortality, politics, public health

## Methods

### Study population

In order to assess county-level associations between age-adjusted COVID-19 mortality rates and 2016 & 2020 Presidential election voting results within the state of Colorado, we selected an ecologic study design. There are a total of 64 counties in the state of Colorado. Inclusion in the study was based on availability of COVID-19 mortality data for each county in a given year. Mortality data from 48 Colorado counties were available for 2020, data from 56 counties were available for 2021, and data from 49 counties were available for 2022. We selected county level analysis as we hypothesize that within the context of a respiratory pathogen, exposure and risk may be defined by the health behaviors of those in the surrounding community in addition to the choices made by individuals. As discussed in the introduction, county-level decisions also became critical during the pandemic.

### Exposure of interest

Utilizing data from the Colorado Secretary of State, a binary exposure variable was constructed as an indicator of the voting outcome in each county in the 2020 Presidential election. Counties that Trump won were assigned the exposure, while counties Joseph Biden won were considered unexposed. Every county in the state voted in highest percentage for one of those candidates during the election, and as such, there were no additional candidates to use in this comparison.23,24

### Outcomes of interest

The outcomes of interest were the age-adjusted annual COVID-19 mortality rates in 2020, 2021, and 2022. International Classification of Disease, 10th edition (ICD-10) Code U07.1 was used as the identification criterion for death certificates, indicating cases where COVID-19 was listed as the primary or underlying cause of death. Mortality data were obtained from the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (CDPHE). Under CDPHE suppression rules, data for counties with 2 or fewer deaths in a given calendar year were unavailable, which primarily impacted counties with small populations. CDPHE used the 2000 United States Census to calculate the age-adjusted rates based on the counts using standardization.

### Covariate

To account for potential confounding resulting from county level differences in demographic variables, we selected the demographics percentile from the Colorado EnviroScreen Environmental Justice tool for use in adjusted models.25 Colorado EnviroScreen is an interactive environmental justice mapping tool created by CDPHE that uses data from 35 different metrics to construct scores used to compare the overall burden from 1 county to the next within the state. There is an overall score available for each county as well as sub-scores for groups of components. The demographics percentile metric was chosen for inclusion in this study because it incorporates information on county-level income, disability, language, housing burden, race, and ethnicity, allowing for efficient adjustment for multiple variations in population and socio-economic factors simultaneously. (More description of Colorado EnviroScreen methodology is available in the Supplemental materials.)25

### Statistical analysis

Due to overdispersion in the mortality data, negative binomial regression models were selected and constructed separately for each year of outcome data (2020, 2021, and 2022), regressed against the binary indicator for election outcome in 2020, resulting in a total of 3 exposure/outcome models for the analysis. In addition to the binary exposure variable, all models were adjusted using the demographics percentile from Colorado EnviroScreen and included a population offset term to account for the wide variation in county level population. The offset term was calculated using the CDPHE provided age-adjusted mortality rate multiplied times the provided annual population in each county, then divided by 100 000. The resulting value is an age-adjusted count for deaths in each county, which is then modeled with an offset based on the total population in that county. Models with a population offset term were selected as primary due to better model fit a measured by AIC and BIC compared to models without the offset term.

As a sensitivity analysis and in comparison to the negative binomial results, adjusted models were built using Quasi-Poisson regression, again including a population offset term. Negative binomial and Quasi-Poisson regression methods are both appropriate for use in situations where overdispersion is present in the data, as was the case regarding the COVID-19 mortality outcome data.26

We recognize that use of 2020 election data may introduce concerns regarding temporality, as most of the year had already occurred, including 8 months of the pandemic, at the time of the election, and it is possible that the pandemic itself had influence on the outcome of that election. In consideration of this reality, models using 2016 election data for the exposure instead of 2020 were constructed for a second sensitivity analysis, and the correlation between 2016 and 2020 election data was assessed using a Spearman test.

Finally, a third sensitivity analysis used a continuous vote percentage as the exposure rather than a binary indicator, modeled for a 10% increase in the vote for Trump, adjusting for demographics.

Statistical analyses were primarily performed in R, version 4.3.1, with some preliminary data cleaning conducted using Microsoft Excel. The present study was reviewed by the University Institutional Review Board, Biomedical Division and deemed not to be human subjects research. Protocol 4034, determination date December 1, 2022. The datasets generated and analyzed for the current study are available in Dryad Data Repository, DOI: 10.5061/dryad.573n5tbfh.

## Results

In the 2020 Presidential election, Trump won 40 counties in Colorado, while Biden won 24. Although Trump won more counties, the mean county population was over 3 times higher in counties that Biden won than in counties that Trump won. Mean mortality values for counties Trump won were higher than in counties Biden won for all years of the outcome data. Age-adjusted county-level annual COVID-19 mortality rates over the 3-year study period ranged from 14.3 to 446.8 per 100 000, with the highest rates occurring in 2021. The first sensitivity analysis used adjusted Quasi-Poisson models with a population offset, which again yielded statistically significant findings for 2021 mortality, though attenuated from the negative binomial model results. Although point estimates indicated a slightly negative association for 2020 and a slightly positive association for 2022 data, confidence intervals for both years included the null. (Quasi-Poisson results are available in Supplemental Table S2, available at [http://links.lww.com/JPHMP/B456](http://links.lww.com/JPHMP/B456)).

Regarding the choice of election data, our second sensitivity analysis compared years of election data. A Spearman test comparing the 2 years of election data was found to have a positive correlation of 0.87, with 62 degrees of freedom, and a corresponding _P_ value of<.001, indicating there was a high level of agreement between the 2 elections. In 4 counties, election results shifted parties between parties in the 2016 and 2020 elections, with 3 moving from the Republican party candidate, Trump, to the Democratic party candidate, Biden, and 1 moving in the opposite direction. In comparison with 2020 election models, regression models using 2016 election data instead of 2020 election data yielded similar findings with very slightly attenuated estimates. (2016 election model results are available in Supplemental Table S3, available at [http://links.lww.com/JPHMP/B456](http://links.lww.com/JPHMP/B456)).

Finally, modeling election data as a continuous variable in our third sensitivity analysis instead of a binary variable resulted in positive, statistically significant associations for all years. A 10% increase in the county-level vote percentage for Trump was found to be associated with between 13% and 21% increased COVID-19 mortality. (Continuous model results are available in Supplemental Table S4, available at [http://links.lww.com/JPHMP/B456](http://links.lww.com/JPHMP/B456)).

## Discussion

We found a statistically significant association between county-level political environment as measured by election results and age-adjusted COVID-19 mortality rates in 2021 which was robust to all methods of sensitivity analyses and adds to a growing body of evidence that political environment was associated with COVID-19 mortality in Colorado. In Colorado, counties voting for Trump experienced nearly twice the COVID-19 mortality rate in 2021. Significant results were not identified for COVID-19 mortality in the other years of the pandemic studied.

Variation in associations by year may be attributed to a number of factors. In the first year of the pandemic, politics appeared to impact mitigation measures, social distancing, mask mandates, closures, and remote schooling decisions.7 In this early stage, it is possible that COVID-19 mortality data are not accurate due to lack of available tests and inconsistent reporting.16 Further in the second and third year of the pandemic, the influence of political ideation appeared to be primarily concerned with influencing vaccination status. The relationship between county level vaccination rates and mortality has been demonstrated.27 A possible explanation for the nonsignificant findings in 2022 mortality may be related to the depletion of susceptibles both in terms of vaccination status and mortality from the virus.28,29 As time progressed, there were fewer and fewer unvaccinated people and those most vulnerable might have already succumbed to the virus.

The relationship between political environment and COVID-19 mortality appears to be mediated by vaccination. In essence this means that vaccination is on a causal pathway between the 2, explaining at least some of the association. This relationship is supported by the 2023 findings of Alemi and Lee, who studied the mediation effect for vaccines in COVID-19.30 Given the likely role of vaccination as a mediator, vaccination rates were not included separately as a predictor in the model because doing so would block the portion of the association on that mediated pathway. (A directed acyclic graph is included in the Supplemental Materials, Figure S1, available at [http://links.lww.com/JPHMP/B456](http://links.lww.com/JPHMP/B456), demonstrating included variables and the vaccine mediated pathway).

Election data are only made available aggregated by geography, the smallest unit of which is the county level in Colorado. Individual level data are not available and can only be estimated through reliance on polls. Although sometimes used to measure political environment, party affiliation was not selected as the exposure for this study with intention given that a high percentage of unaffiliated voters are registered in Colorado. Laws in the state allow unaffiliated individuals to vote in primaries, reducing the need to choose a formal affiliation.31,32 Because county-level officials hold office in a non-partisan fashion in Colorado, there is no way to assess the connection between their decisions related to mitigation, education, vaccination promotion and their political affiliations. In light of the above considerations, we determined that aggregated presidential vote data were an appropriate proxy for political environment at the county level.

We analyzed the association here using both 2016 and 2020 election data with intention to capture how, if at all, these relationships may have differed. Correlation results indicated a high level of agreement between the election data; however, these data are not fully correlated. Creating separate models for each year of election data allowed determination of whether those small differences in the election data year to year resulted in meaningful changes to the association with COVID-19 mortality. If only 2016 election data were utilized, results may not have captured the full impact of the county-level political environment closer to the outcome years under study. Likewise, using only the 2020 election data might have created the above mentioned temporality concerns. The choice here to include both years provides broader information for the exploration of these associations, and overall, primary models built using the 2020 election exposure tended to have slightly stronger point estimates than sensitivity models using the 2016 election exposure, though the findings were largely in agreement.

Although the continuous models in the third sensitivity analysis provide valuable information about the connection between vote percentage and mortality, they were not selected as the primary models here because they are not tied to the actual election outcome for each county, reflecting only the linear relationship between the variables.

### Strengths of this study

Data were made available from CDPHE as age-adjusted rates, which automatically addresses the confounder of the populational age distribution at the county level. The use of the Colorado EnviroScreen demographics percentile as a covariate in this analysis is a strength. Although Colorado EnviroScreen was created for environmental justice applications for the community, agencies, and governmental institutions, this study demonstrates the utility of the composite demographics measures as a way to efficiently adjust for multiple county-level confounders at once in health research. Additional strengths of this study include state-wide analysis and the utilization of publicly available data sources. The agreement in the results using different modeling techniques, including those in the sensitivity analysis lend robustness to the findings and increases confidence in the associations found regarding 2021 COVID-19 mortality.

### Limitations of this study

Using an ecologic study, we are limited here in interpretation, knowing these findings cannot be extrapolated to the individual level. This analysis focused on the county level with intention due to our interest in the influence of community level exposures. Residual confounding for the variables included in the demographics score as well as unmeasured confounding are always a possibility. We hypothesize that it would be highly unlikely for any additional predictor to have a strong enough relationship to negate the associations found in this study. We recognize that people who live and work in different counties exist, which may result in some exposure misclassification, though any misclassification present as a result would most likely be nondifferential given that crossing county boundaries for work does not occur in a differential manner. In terms of selection bias, the exclusion of counties with missing data is not likely to be very influential in this study. Most counties representing a total of 98.4% of the overall state population were included in the analysis.

It is possible that use of ICD codes to determine COVID-19 mortality resulted in substantially undercounting actual deaths, potentially including the limitation of only counting patients where COVID-19 was listed as the underlying cause of death. Rural areas in Colorado are more likely to have coroners versus medical examiners, and it has been established that coroners are more likely to make errors in cause of death determinations.33 Coroners are frequently chosen through elections in Colorado and as such might have been open to influence from regional politics as a result.34 It is therefore possible that some misclassification of the outcome occurred here, and if so, there is a further possibility that misclassification would be differential. The directionality of this misclassification would lead us, perhaps, to an even stronger association. There is also a possibility that the number of deaths was even higher than documented in 2020 due to the evolving status of the COVID-19 pandemic and early lack of available tests. Some have argued that it might be a more accurate measure to utilize data on excess mortality rather than focus solely on deaths specifically coded for COVID-19 to more fully capture the mortality effects of the pandemic.35,36

In the present ecologic study, we cannot determine the influence of individual level political views or how those individual views may influence the county-wide environment because only aggregated election data were utilized here. Additionally, the specific findings of one study using voter registration data rather than election data found that individual political affiliation was associated with excess deaths during the COVID-19.19 The present research finds similar associations using actual election data rather than voter registration, perhaps adding some evidence of the similarity of both measures to describe community level political environment. Ideally, future research would look at the combined influence of both individual and community level political views on health outcomes, including COVID-19 specific mortality and excess mortality rates.

An additional limitation of this study is that our specific findings may not be generalizable to states outside of Colorado. Although the results here align with other similar studies,19,20 the characteristics of each state are unique in terms of population demographics and distribution, the political environment, and the nature of voter registration requirements. We believe that use of actual voting data is more directly relevant to research in Colorado because so many voters in Colorado are unaffiliated.

## Conclusion

This study finds an ecologic association between county-level political environment and COVID-19 mortality. As we move into the endemic period in COVID-19’s history, exploring the differences of COVID-19 mortality is necessary to inform future decisions. If political environment truly is associated with COVID-19 mortality, as our findings indicate, intentional work to restore and build faith and trust in the public health system is essential.37 There is a real opportunity here to learn from this experience and to address some of the most critical needs as we emerge from the COVID-19 pandemic. To best build the collaborative relationships necessary for a responsive and equitable public health system, we encourage open dialogue and engagement among policymakers, employers, public health agencies, health care groups, advocacy groups, and community partners about the drivers of health outcomes in the most transparent manner possible to allow for shared priority setting, coordination, education and planning.38 Working toward better collaboration between the medical care system and the public health system will better position us all for the next pandemic.39

This study provides an opportunity to learn from and to address some critical needs in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic that may support future public health infectious disease planning efforts. Given the realities of climate change and of living in a global economy, this likely will not be our last pandemic. Within the context of COVID-19 and other infectious disease, this carries implications for the importance of health education and mitigation strategies as well as vaccination approaches. If politics are indeed a predictor for health outcomes such as COVID-19 mortality, it is possible that this relationship between political environment and outcomes exists for more health conditions than we are aware, and additional study into the relationships between political environment and other health outcomes, both related to communicable and non-communicable diseases, should be pursued. Moving forward, perhaps the lesson here is that it may be beneficial for both researchers and public health practitioners to view political environment as a potential predictor of health outcomes in an effort to better assess risk, develop mitigation strategies as needed, and design meaningful communication, collaboration and education that are consistent across party lines.40 Implications for Policy & Practice The identification of political environment as a predictor of risk builds awareness of this factor’s influence on both individuals and communities and should provide motivation for robust, clear, and intentional health education and communication.As COVID-19 transitions toward endemicity and we confront the reality that this will not be our last pandemic, public health agencies and governmental institutions need to understand the relationship between politics and health outcomes; this study may foster the creation of unique opportunities for vital community liaisons and trusted messengers to help bridge communication gaps.This study’s findings urge cooperation and collaboration between community member and partners, researchers, public health agencies, governmental bodies, educational institutions, industry, media, and other stakeholders—and should inform interactions between these groups with the overarching goal of shared decision-making, informed by scientific methods and public health ethics principles.

# Mountain West states’ COVID-19 death rates stand out in new analysis

KUNR Public Radio | By [Kaleb Roedel](https://www.kunr.org/people/kaleb-roedel)

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

The national COVID-19 death rate between January 2020 and July 2022 was 372 deaths per 100,000 people, [according to a study](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(23)00461-0/fulltext#%20) published in _The Lancet_ last week.

## A new analysis shows that states in the Mountain West suffered some of the highest COVID-19 death rates in the U.S. between January 2020 and July 2022.

The national average was 372 deaths from COVID-19 per 100,000 people, [according to a study](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(23)00461-0/fulltext#%20) published in _The Lancet_ last week.

Arizona’s rate was 581 deaths per 100,000 people – the highest in the nation. New Mexico had the third-highest rate with 521 deaths per 100,000 people.

The death rates were also well above the national average in the other Mountain West states: Colorado (473 per 100,000), Idaho (469), Utah (467), Nevada (453), Wyoming (422) and Montana (420).

That’s partly because many Mountain West states are “frontier-minded,” said Emma Castro, a researcher at the Institute of Health Metrics and Evaluation at the University of Washington.

“The states were more reticent to use mandates, and felt that it was up to the individual to decide what mitigating measures they wanted to take to protect themselves against COVID,” Castro said.

The study, which assessed pandemic policies and behaviors, shows states that implemented more mask and vaccine mandates had lower infection rates. Moreover, lower COVID death rates were found in states with higher levels of education, lower levels of poverty, and more trust in the federal government and scientific community. Nationwide, Hawaii had the lowest rates at 147 deaths per 100,000, followed by New Hampshire (215) and Maine (281).

Castro noted that states with a larger share of the population identifying as Black, Hispanic, or American Indian and Alaska Native tended to have higher infection rates.

# Mountain West states’ COVID-19 death rates stand out in new analysis

KUNR Public Radio | By [Kaleb Roedel](https://www.kunr.org/people/kaleb-roedel)

 Published March 29, 2023 at 4:20 PM PDT

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

The national COVID-19 death rate between January 2020 and July 2022 was 372 deaths per 100,000 people, [according to a study](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(23)00461-0/fulltext#%20) published in _The Lancet_ last week.

## A new analysis shows that states in the Mountain West suffered some of the highest COVID-19 death rates in the U.S. between January 2020 and July 2022.

The national average was 372 deaths from COVID-19 per 100,000 people, [according to a study](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(23)00461-0/fulltext#%20) published in _The Lancet_ last week.

Arizona’s rate was 581 deaths per 100,000 people – the highest in the nation. New Mexico had the third-highest rate with 521 deaths per 100,000 people.

The death rates were also well above the national average in the other Mountain West states: Colorado (473 per 100,000), Idaho (469), Utah (467), Nevada (453), Wyoming (422) and Montana (420).

That’s partly because many Mountain West states are “frontier-minded,” said Emma Castro, a researcher at the Institute of Health Metrics and Evaluation at the University of Washington.

“The states were more reticent to use mandates, and felt that it was up to the individual to decide what mitigating measures they wanted to take to protect themselves against COVID,” Castro said.

The study, which assessed pandemic policies and behaviors, shows states that implemented more mask and vaccine mandates had lower infection rates. Moreover, lower COVID death rates were found in states with higher levels of education, lower levels of poverty, and more trust in the federal government and scientific community. Nationwide, Hawaii had the lowest rates at 147 deaths per 100,000, followed by New Hampshire (215) and Maine (281).

Castro noted that states with a larger share of the population identifying as Black, Hispanic, or American Indian and Alaska Native tended to have higher infection rates.

Projections and scenarios

We produce six scenarios when projecting COVID-19. The reference scenario is our forecast of what we think
is most likely to happen. We assume that if the daily mortality rate from COVID-19 reaches 8 per million,
social distancing (SD) mandates will be re-imposed. The mandate easing scenario is what would happen if
governments continue to ease social distancing mandates with no re-imposition. The universal mask mandate
scenario is what would happen if mask use increased immediately to 95% and social distancing mandates
were re-imposed at 8 deaths per million. These three scenarios assume our reference vaccine delivery scale up
where vaccine delivery will scale to full capacity over 90 days.
The rapid vaccine rollout scenario assumes that vaccine distribution will scale up to full delivery capacity in
half the time as the reference delivery scenario and that the maximum doses that can be delivered per day is
twice as much as the reference delivery scenario. The rapid vaccine rollout to high-risk populations scenario
is the same but high-risk populations are vaccinated before essential workers or other adults. The no vaccine
scenario is the same as our reference scenario but with no vaccine use.
